2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership

171 172
173 The following is a structured extraction from raw notes, organized by theme. These ideas form the basis of the new design. 174
175 176

Architecture shift

177

Move from a single orchestrator skill with inline stages to a true orchestrator-and-subagents pattern. The orchestrator owns coordination logic and routing decisions. Every stage runs as an isolated subagent with a clean context window. This eliminates context rot, reduces cross-contamination between phases, and makes each agent unit-testable.

178 179

Grooming gets an adversary

180

The current grooming skill self-challenges its own output. That is insufficient for complex or high-risk changes. A dedicated CHALLENGER agent — a skeptical senior engineer — should independently review the grooming plan, looking for hidden assumptions, missing risks, and reasons not to proceed. This agent should not be invoked for every ticket: the orchestrator decides based on the complexity and risk level returned by the GROOMING agent. Trivial fixes skip it entirely. Complex or high-risk plans always go through it, with up to two rounds of back-and-forth before escalating to a human.

181 182

End-to-end testing as a shared primitive

183

End-to-end capability (Playwright for UI, curl/API calls for backends) should not live exclusively in the QA agent. The IMPLEMENTER needs basic E2E validation to confirm its own work before handing off. The GROOMING agent may also use the basic E2E tier to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration. The recommendation: define E2E as a shared skill that multiple agents can access at a basic level, with the QA ENGINEER using an extended version that goes deeper into edge cases, regression scenarios, and visual comparison.

184 185

Context discipline in the orchestrator

186

Every agent invocation must receive exactly the context it needs, no more. The orchestrator is responsible for distilling prior outputs into the minimal structured handoff for each downstream agent. A CHALLENGER needs the ticket and the grooming plan — not the full interaction history leading up to it. A PR REVIEWER only needs the diff, ticket, and conventions — not the grooming discussion. The orchestrator acts as a context editor, not a context relay.

187 188

Structured return contracts

189

Every agent must return a machine-readable structured object (JSON) directly to the orchestrator. The orchestrator receives the return value, makes a routing decision, and passes only the relevant fields to the next agent. Each agent's contract is defined by its output schema: specific fields, specific value ranges, specific verdict flags. Natural language is for human-facing summaries only — the routing logic runs on the structured part.

190

Agents that produce reviews, challenges, or assessments classify each feedback item with a priority tier: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional enhancement). The orchestrator uses this classification to route: MUST_HAVE items drive loop-back or escalation logic; SHOULD_HAVE and below items that are not blocking are dispatched to the TICKET agent as parallel, non-blocking follow-up tasks. The main pipeline does not wait for these secondary tasks.

191 192

Risk-based routing

193

The orchestrator adjusts the pipeline dynamically based on what it learns at each stage. All routing decisions happen after the GROOMING agent returns, never before. Key routing signals: effort size (XL → always invoke CHALLENGER), risk level from GROOMING (HIGH → always invoke CHALLENGER), blocker criticality from PR REVIEWER (CRITICAL → pause for human, HIGH → loop to implementer), QA result (FAIL → loop to implementer before escalating).

194 195

Loop-back protocols

196

Feedback loops should be first-class pipeline primitives, not manual workarounds. GROOMING ↔ CHALLENGER loops (max 2 rounds for NEEDS_REVISION, 1 round for BLOCKED), IMPLEMENTER ↔ PR REVIEWER loops (max 1 round per blocker criticality tier), and IMPLEMENTER ↔ QA ENGINEER loops are modelled explicitly in the orchestrator's logic with round counters and escalation conditions.

197 198

Continuous updates of Git tools

199

Agents must report their work just like humans do on GitHub or GitLab: issues, comments for grooming, pull requests, etc. Each agent is responsible for handling its own Git operations. The orchestrator can route nice to havs and feedback for later to the ticket writer so they are stored in the backlog, without stopping the main flow.

200 201

AI transparency

202

All AI-generated content written to external systems (GitHub issues, GitLab tickets, PR descriptions, MR descriptions) must carry a clearly visible AI-generated notice. All commits must include a Co-Authored-By tag. This applies to everything the pipeline writes, without exception, and is enforced by the agents themselves.

203 204

Generic + customizable

205

The pipeline ships as a reusable template that any team can adopt out of the box. The only component that should be team-specific is the IMPLEMENTER agent, which needs to know the codebase conventions, tech stack, test commands, and team patterns. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend and backend, for instance — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents. All other agents work generically without customization.

206 207

3. State of the art: what the field has learned

208 209
210 Several converging findings from 2025–2026 production agentic systems directly inform this design. The key insight: architecture matters more than model choice. The gap between a 10% productivity improvement and a 25–30% improvement is not model capability — it is context engineering. 211
212 213

Context rot is real and architectural

214

Chroma Research (2025) demonstrated that LLM performance degrades consistently as input tokens increase, even on simple tasks, and degrades faster on multi-step reasoning. This is context rot. It means a single agent that accumulates the full history of an exploration session, planning debates, and test failures will produce worse output at the PR review stage than a fresh agent given only the relevant context. The solution is architectural: subagent isolation, not larger context windows.

215

A correlated finding: agents miss relevant context 56% of the time when relying on on-demand retrieval. This makes explicit structured handoffs — where the orchestrator packages exactly what each agent needs — far more reliable than letting agents fetch their own context from conversation history.

216 217

The adversarial review pattern reduces errors and cost

218

Production systems (notably Hugues Clouâtre's architecture, deployed across multiple Rust projects) use a SCOUT + GUARD pattern: an exploratory agent produces a research report, and a smaller adversarial agent stress-tests it before a planner synthesizes both. Finding flaws in a concrete proposal requires less reasoning range than producing one — which means a smaller, cheaper model can handle adversarial review effectively. This is why the CHALLENGER agent in this design can be a smaller model, while the GROOMING agent must be a capable one.

219 220

Structured JSON return contracts are the coordination layer

221

The field has converged on typed JSON as the communication protocol between agents. Agents return structured objects directly to the orchestrator rather than persisting files or sharing conversation history. Three practical reasons: the contracts are auditable (every decision is recorded in the orchestrator's context), resumable (any session can be restarted from a checkpoint), and debuggable (failures include exact locations and actionable next steps). This design defines a typed JSON schema for every agent's output, passed as a return value through the orchestrator.

222 223

Unstructured multi-agent networks amplify errors

224

Research on multi-agent LLM pipelines found that unstructured networks amplify errors up to 17.2× compared to single-agent baselines. When agents are chained without explicit topology and structured communication contracts, each agent's output noise becomes the next agent's input noise. Every agent-to-agent interaction in this design must have a typed schema, not natural language.

225 226

Model routing reduces cost without sacrificing quality

227

Using capable models for planning and reasoning-intensive tasks, and faster/cheaper models for execution-intensive tasks, can reduce API costs by 50–60% versus an all-capable-model approach. The GROOMING agent and ORCHESTRATOR need the most reasoning capability. The CHALLENGER, IMPLEMENTER's basic checks, and the DOD checker can route to faster models.

228 229

AGENTS.md as the shared knowledge layer

230

Vercel's evals (2026) showed that a well-written AGENTS.md file achieved 100% pass rate on build, lint, and test tasks where skill-based approaches maxed out at 79%. Every subagent in this system inherits project context through the project instructions file — not through an explicit handoff every time. This is the "CSS for agents" pattern: global rules cascade into every subagent automatically.

231 232

2026 focus: harnesses, not just agents

233

The engineering emphasis in 2026 has shifted from building individual agents to building the environments, verification loops, and supervision layers that make agents reliable at scale. The orchestrator in this design is the harness: its job is supervision, routing, loop management, and escalation — not execution. Execution is fully delegated to isolated agents.

4. New system design

236 237
238 The new system replaces the linear skill chain with a fully agentic orchestrator-and-subagents architecture. The orchestrator is the only persistent context. All stages run as isolated agents that receive a structured input and return a structured output. The orchestrator reads the output, makes a routing decision, and invokes the next agent — or loops back, or escalates. Two agents always run: TICKET and GROOMING. All other agents are conditional based on what GROOMING returns. 239

Internal design document · Engineering AI Systems

Agentic Delivery Pipeline v2.1

Prepared May 2026 · Based on gas-delivery-pipeline-templates plugin + state-of-the-art research

Contents

  1. Current state: what we have
  2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership
  3. State of the art: what the field has learned
  4. New system design
  5. Agent catalog: responsibilities & contracts
  6. Agent communication schemas
  7. Orchestrator routing logic
  8. Runtime scenarios
  9. AI transparency policy
  10. Standard skills: duplication detection & E2E
  11. Comparison with current systems (WP Rocket, Imagify, BackWPUp)

1. Current state: what we have

The gas-delivery-pipeline-templates plugin is a working linear pipeline driven by a single orchestrator skill. It covers the full engineering lifecycle from raw description to QA validation. The system works well. The question is not whether to replace it, but how to make it genuinely agentic — moving from a chain of sequential skills to an adaptive, self-routing network of specialized agents.

The current pipeline runs in a fixed linear sequence:

The pipeline is strong but has two structural limitations. First, the orchestrator is reactive, not adaptive: it follows a fixed sequence with manual pause points rather than routing dynamically based on what each agent produces. Second, the quality gates (grooming, review-pr) have no feedback loops — when grooming identifies a high-risk plan, there is no mechanism to challenge it before handing off to implementation.

ComponentCurrent formLimitation
delivery-orchestrationSkill (inline, linear)No adaptive routing, no risk-based branching
ticket-writerSkill (inline)No structured JSON output for downstream agents
groomingSkill (inline, single-pass)No codebase exploration phase, no adversarial review, no challenger agent
implementationMain agent (same context)No E2E capability, no self-run DOD check, not isolated
technical-documentationSkill (inline)Fine as-is
dodSkill (inline, orchestrator-run)Output is prose, not machine-readable; single layer only
open-prSkill (inline)No AI transparency annotation
review-prSubagent (isolated)No criticality tiers, no inline comment posting, no loop-back protocol
qa-engineerSubagent (isolated)No shared E2E primitive, Playwright only in QA, no test authoring obligation

2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership

The following is a structured extraction from raw notes, organized by theme. These ideas form the basis of the new design.

Architecture shift

Move from a single orchestrator skill with inline stages to a true orchestrator-and-subagents pattern. The orchestrator owns coordination logic and routing decisions. Every stage runs as an isolated subagent with a clean context window. This eliminates context rot, reduces cross-contamination between phases, and makes each agent unit-testable.

Grooming gets an adversary

The current grooming skill self-challenges its own output. That is insufficient for complex or high-risk changes. A dedicated CHALLENGER agent — a skeptical senior engineer — should independently review the grooming plan, looking for hidden assumptions, missing risks, and reasons not to proceed. This agent should not be invoked for every ticket: the orchestrator decides based on the complexity and risk level returned by the GROOMING agent. Trivial fixes skip it entirely. Complex or high-risk plans always go through it, with up to two rounds of back-and-forth before escalating to a human.

End-to-end testing as a shared primitive

End-to-end capability (Playwright for UI, curl/API calls for backends) should not live exclusively in the QA agent. The IMPLEMENTER needs basic E2E validation to confirm its own work before handing off. The GROOMING agent may also use the basic E2E tier to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration. The recommendation: define E2E as a shared skill that multiple agents can access at a basic level, with the QA ENGINEER using an extended version that goes deeper into edge cases, regression scenarios, and visual comparison.

Context discipline in the orchestrator

Every agent invocation must receive exactly the context it needs, no more. The orchestrator is responsible for distilling prior outputs into the minimal structured handoff for each downstream agent. A CHALLENGER needs the ticket and the grooming plan — not the full interaction history leading up to it. A PR REVIEWER only needs the diff, ticket, and conventions — not the grooming discussion. The orchestrator acts as a context editor, not a context relay.

Structured return contracts

Every agent must return a machine-readable structured object (JSON) directly to the orchestrator. The orchestrator receives the return value, makes a routing decision, and passes only the relevant fields to the next agent. Each agent's contract is defined by its output schema: specific fields, specific value ranges, specific verdict flags. Natural language is for human-facing summaries only — the routing logic runs on the structured part.

Agents that produce reviews, challenges, or assessments classify each feedback item with a priority tier: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional enhancement). The orchestrator uses this classification to route: MUST_HAVE items drive loop-back or escalation logic; SHOULD_HAVE and below items that are not blocking are dispatched to the TICKET agent as parallel, non-blocking follow-up tasks. The main pipeline does not wait for these secondary tasks.

Risk-based routing

The orchestrator adjusts the pipeline dynamically based on what it learns at each stage. All routing decisions happen after the GROOMING agent returns, never before. Key routing signals: effort size (XL → always invoke CHALLENGER), risk level from GROOMING (HIGH → always invoke CHALLENGER), blocker criticality from PR REVIEWER (CRITICAL → pause for human, HIGH → loop to implementer), QA result (FAIL → loop to implementer before escalating).

Loop-back protocols

Feedback loops should be first-class pipeline primitives, not manual workarounds. GROOMING ↔ CHALLENGER loops (max 2 rounds for NEEDS_REVISION, 1 round for BLOCKED), IMPLEMENTER ↔ PR REVIEWER loops (max 1 round per blocker criticality tier), and IMPLEMENTER ↔ QA ENGINEER loops are modelled explicitly in the orchestrator's logic with round counters and escalation conditions.

Continuous updates of Git tools

Agents must report their work just like humans do on GitHub or GitLab: issues, comments for grooming, pull requests, etc. Each agent is responsible for handling its own Git operations. The orchestrator can route nice to havs and feedback for later to the ticket writer so they are stored in the backlog, without stopping the main flow.

AI transparency

All AI-generated content written to external systems (GitHub issues, GitLab tickets, PR descriptions, MR descriptions) must carry a clearly visible AI-generated notice. All commits must include a Co-Authored-By tag. This applies to everything the pipeline writes, without exception, and is enforced by the agents themselves.

Generic + customizable

The pipeline ships as a reusable template that any team can adopt out of the box. The only component that should be team-specific is the IMPLEMENTER agent, which needs to know the codebase conventions, tech stack, test commands, and team patterns. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend and backend, for instance — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents. All other agents work generically without customization.

3. State of the art: what the field has learned

Several converging findings from 2025–2026 production agentic systems directly inform this design. The key insight: architecture matters more than model choice. The gap between a 10% productivity improvement and a 25–30% improvement is not model capability — it is context engineering.

Context rot is real and architectural

Chroma Research (2025) demonstrated that LLM performance degrades consistently as input tokens increase, even on simple tasks, and degrades faster on multi-step reasoning. This is context rot. It means a single agent that accumulates the full history of an exploration session, planning debates, and test failures will produce worse output at the PR review stage than a fresh agent given only the relevant context. The solution is architectural: subagent isolation, not larger context windows.

A correlated finding: agents miss relevant context 56% of the time when relying on on-demand retrieval. This makes explicit structured handoffs — where the orchestrator packages exactly what each agent needs — far more reliable than letting agents fetch their own context from conversation history.

The adversarial review pattern reduces errors and cost

Production systems (notably Hugues Clouâtre's architecture, deployed across multiple Rust projects) use a SCOUT + GUARD pattern: an exploratory agent produces a research report, and a smaller adversarial agent stress-tests it before a planner synthesizes both. Finding flaws in a concrete proposal requires less reasoning range than producing one — which means a smaller, cheaper model can handle adversarial review effectively. This is why the CHALLENGER agent in this design can be a smaller model, while the GROOMING agent must be a capable one.

Structured JSON return contracts are the coordination layer

The field has converged on typed JSON as the communication protocol between agents. Agents return structured objects directly to the orchestrator rather than persisting files or sharing conversation history. Three practical reasons: the contracts are auditable (every decision is recorded in the orchestrator's context), resumable (any session can be restarted from a checkpoint), and debuggable (failures include exact locations and actionable next steps). This design defines a typed JSON schema for every agent's output, passed as a return value through the orchestrator.

Unstructured multi-agent networks amplify errors

Research on multi-agent LLM pipelines found that unstructured networks amplify errors up to 17.2× compared to single-agent baselines. When agents are chained without explicit topology and structured communication contracts, each agent's output noise becomes the next agent's input noise. Every agent-to-agent interaction in this design must have a typed schema, not natural language.

Model routing reduces cost without sacrificing quality

Using capable models for planning and reasoning-intensive tasks, and faster/cheaper models for execution-intensive tasks, can reduce API costs by 50–60% versus an all-capable-model approach. The GROOMING agent and ORCHESTRATOR need the most reasoning capability. The CHALLENGER, IMPLEMENTER's basic checks, and the DOD checker can route to faster models.

AGENTS.md as the shared knowledge layer

Vercel's evals (2026) showed that a well-written AGENTS.md file achieved 100% pass rate on build, lint, and test tasks where skill-based approaches maxed out at 79%. Every subagent in this system inherits project context through the project instructions file — not through an explicit handoff every time. This is the "CSS for agents" pattern: global rules cascade into every subagent automatically.

2026 focus: harnesses, not just agents

The engineering emphasis in 2026 has shifted from building individual agents to building the environments, verification loops, and supervision layers that make agents reliable at scale. The orchestrator in this design is the harness: its job is supervision, routing, loop management, and escalation — not execution. Execution is fully delegated to isolated agents.

4. New system design

The new system replaces the linear skill chain with a fully agentic orchestrator-and-subagents architecture. The orchestrator is the only persistent context. All stages run as isolated agents that receive a structured input and return a structured output. The orchestrator reads the output, makes a routing decision, and invokes the next agent — or loops back, or escalates. Two agents always run: TICKET and GROOMING. All other agents are conditional based on what GROOMING returns.

System overview

Key architectural decisions

The orchestrator owns routing, not execution. The orchestrator's only job is to read structured return values from agents, make routing decisions, and invoke the next agent with the right minimal context. It never runs code, writes files, or produces content itself.

TICKET and GROOMING always run. These are the two mandatory stages in every pipeline run. All other routing decisions — whether to invoke CHALLENGER, PR REVIEWER, dedicated QA, or DOCS — are made post-grooming using grooming.risk_level, grooming.effort, and the grooming.risk_notes prose field. Nothing is routed before the grooming output is available.

DOCS, DOD, and PR OPENER are IMPLEMENTER skills, not orchestrator-dispatched agents. The IMPLEMENTER runs these as inline steps before handing off. It updates docs, runs a first DOD check (layer 1) and self-corrects any issues it can resolve, then opens the PR. The orchestrator runs a second independent DOD gate (layer 2) before invoking the PR REVIEWER. This two-layer approach catches issues the IMPLEMENTER missed without requiring a separate agent dispatch for routine work.

Non-blocking NTH dispatch. When any agent returns COULD_HAVE or NICE_TO_HAVE feedback items, the orchestrator dispatches the TICKET agent to create follow-up tickets for those items as a parallel, non-blocking task. The main pipeline continues immediately without waiting.

E2E as a shared primitive. Playwright and API-call capability is available to any agent that needs it via a shared E2E skill. The GROOMING agent and IMPLEMENTER use a basic version (behavioral verification and smoke tests). The QA ENGINEER uses an extended version covering full acceptance criteria, regression, visual comparison, and edge cases.

5. Agent catalog

Each agent is defined by its type (subagent in isolated context, or skill running inline), its required input, its output schema, its routing authority, and its AI transparency obligations. GROOMING combines codebase exploration and planning in a single isolated pass. DOCS, DOD, and PR OPENER run as inline skills inside the IMPLEMENTER.
Orchestrator ORCHESTRATOR persistent context no execution

Responsibility: Receive the initial input, determine pipeline scope, invoke agents in order, evaluate structured return values, route forward or loop back, escalate to human when routing rules are exhausted.

Model: Capable reasoning model (Sonnet-class or above). Temperature: 0.2 — routing decisions should be consistent, not creative.

Does not: Execute code. Write files. Produce content. Generate issues or PRs directly.

Routing authority: All routing decisions happen after GROOMING returns. The orchestrator reads grooming.risk_level, grooming.effort, and grooming.risk_notes to decide whether to invoke CHALLENGER. Decides loop-back based on review.blockers[*].criticality and qa.overall. Runs the independent DOD layer-2 gate after the IMPLEMENTER hands off. Escalates to human when loop counters are exhausted — always with 1–2 concrete next steps sourced from agent output. Dispatches TICKET agent in parallel for any COULD_HAVE or NICE_TO_HAVE feedback items returned by CHALLENGER, PR REVIEWER, or QA ENGINEER. Once the task is completed and the agentic system stops, the orchestrator returns a structured report to the user with links to the issue & PR, conclusions of each reviewer agents (grooming reviewer, pr reviewer, qa), possible gaps & risks, next steps and follow-up tickets created in any. The report is posted on the main ticket on the git tool as well.

Evolved TICKET agent subagent isolated context always runs

Input: Raw description — prompt, Slack thread, Confluence page, URL, verbal notes. Can also receive a structured NTH feedback item from the orchestrator for follow-up ticket creation.

Output: Structured ticket object. Creates the issue in GitHub/GitLab with AI-generated notice.

AI transparency: All created issues include a notice at the top: "⚠️ This issue was generated with AI assistance. Review before acting."

Model: Fast model sufficient. Temperature: 0.3.

Evolved GROOMING agent subagent explore + plan always runs

Responsibility: A single isolated agent that performs codebase exploration and planning in one pass. It reads files freely, iterates between discovery and reasoning, selects an approach, and produces a structured plan with risk assessment. It does not implement anything. The grooming plan is posted as a comment on the ticket or edited if this is an iteration.

Input: Ticket object from TICKET agent + read-only codebase access.

Output: Grooming object — relevant files, chosen approach, development steps, test plan, risks with severity, effort estimate, risk level, risk_notes prose field, and open questions.

Key output fields: risk_level and effort are the primary routing signals the orchestrator uses post-grooming. risk_notes is a short prose field: confidence level, key risks, anything the orchestrator should weight when making conditional routing decisions.

Model: Capable reasoning model. Temperature: 0.4 — exploratory enough to find non-obvious patterns, focused enough for structured output.

Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash (read-only commands). E2E capability (basic tier) — to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration when needed.

New CHALLENGER agent conditional risk ≥ MEDIUM or effort ≥ L adversarial

Role: A skeptical senior engineer whose only job is to find good reasons not to proceed with the plan as written. Not creative, not constructive — adversarial. Surfaces hidden risks, challenges assumptions, identifies missing steps, proposes alternative approaches. The review is posted as a comment on the ticket or edited if this is an iteration.

Input: Ticket object + grooming output. The ticket provides the original requirement context; the grooming output is what the CHALLENGER reviews. Full interaction history is not passed.

Output: Challenge report — verdict (APPROVED / NEEDS_REVISION / BLOCKED), feedback array with MoSCoW severity classification, and — when verdict is not APPROVED — a required alternative_suggestions array with 1–2 concrete alternatives.

Feedback severity tiers: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress — drives verdict to NEEDS_REVISION or BLOCKED), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional). COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE items are dispatched to TICKET agent by the orchestrator as non-blocking follow-up tasks.

Loop protocol: If verdict = NEEDS_REVISION, the orchestrator routes the challenge report back to GROOMING (max 2 rounds). If verdict = BLOCKED, the orchestrator gives GROOMING one revision attempt before escalating to human. All escalations include the challenge report and the alternative_suggestions for human resolution.

Model: Fast model sufficient — finding flaws in a concrete plan is lower-entropy than producing one. Temperature: 0.1 — precise, not creative.

Evolved IMPLEMENTER agent code task team-specific isolated worktree

Responsibility: Isolated code task in a dedicated git worktree that also runs DOCS, DOD (layer 1), and PR OPENER as inline skills before handing off.

Input: Grooming output + ticket object + project instructions (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md).

Internal skill sequence:

  1. Implement the plan from the grooming output. Run unit and integration tests — fix until passing.
  2. Run E2E smoke test (basic tier) — confirm the primary happy path works.
  3. Run DOCS skill — update documentation if public API or configuration changed.
  4. Run DOD skill (layer 1) — evaluate the Definition of Done. If any check FAILs: self-correct and re-run until PASS or WARN.
  5. Run PR OPENER skill — open the PR with AI-generated notice. Add Co-Authored-By to all commits.

Output: Implementation report — branch name, files changed, test results, E2E smoke result, DOD layer-1 result, PR URL.

Sub-agent decomposition: The GAS template ships as a single generic IMPLEMENTER. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend, backend, infrastructure — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents that operate in sequence or in parallel. Each sub-agent follows the same internal skill sequence; the orchestrator treats the combined output as a single implementation report. The WordPress teams at group.one use this pattern.

Team-specific: This is the one agent teams should customize. Each team adds their tech stack, test commands, coding conventions, and linting rules to the project instructions.

AI transparency: All commits must include Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>. Usage of AI must be identified in the PR description. Enforced in the agent's instructions and skills.

New E2E CAPABILITY shared skill not a standalone agent

Basic tier (GROOMING + IMPLEMENTER): Start the dev server. Navigate to the main page. Confirm the feature or current behavior works for the primary happy path. Report PASS/FAIL. This is a behavioral verification or sanity check, not full QA.

Extended tier (QA ENGINEER): Full acceptance criteria validation. Regression testing. Edge cases. Visual comparison against design specs. API validation with error paths. Test authoring: any manually validated flow that lacks an automated test must get one — written, run, and committed before the QA report is finalized.

Shared primitive: Both tiers use Playwright MCP + curl. The difference is scope and depth, not tooling. The skill definition includes depth-level parameters.

Evolved DOD — two-layer gate layer 1: IMPLEMENTER skill (self-correcting) layer 2: orchestrator gate (independent)

Layer 1 (IMPLEMENTER): The IMPLEMENTER runs the DOD skill as step 4 in its internal sequence. If any check fails, the IMPLEMENTER self-corrects — fixing missing tests, updating docs, resolving lint errors — and re-runs before handing off.

Layer 2 (orchestrator): The orchestrator runs a second, independent DOD check after receiving the IMPLEMENTER's handoff. It reads the same checks from a fresh perspective, without the IMPLEMENTER's self-correction bias. overall: FAIL at layer 2 routes back to IMPLEMENTER once (max one loop-back); if it fails again, escalate to human with specific blockers.

Why two layers: Self-correction in context introduces bias — the IMPLEMENTER may be blind to patterns it just created. The orchestrator's independent check catches what the IMPLEMENTER normalized.

Evolved DOCS · PR OPENER IMPLEMENTER inline skills

DOCS: Runs inside the IMPLEMENTER as step 3. Receives the explicit list of changed files from the implementation context rather than inferring from git. Updates only files referenced in the grooming output as touched.

PR OPENER: Runs inside the IMPLEMENTER as step 5, after DOD layer 1 passes. Enforces AI transparency: every PR/MR description includes a clearly visible AI-generated notice at the top. All commits on the branch carry the Co-Authored-By tag. Both are unconditional.

Evolved PR REVIEWER agent subagent isolated context

Responsibility: Reviews the PR diff against the ticket and project conventions. Posts inline comments directly to the PR/MR on GitHub/GitLab, then returns a structured review object to the orchestrator.

Inline comment posting is required, not optional. For each blocker and each nice-to-have with a concrete suggestion, the agent posts an inline comment on the relevant file+line. The structured return value is produced in parallel. Both happen before the agent reports complete.

Criticality tiers:

  • CRITICAL: Security vulnerability or breaking change. Orchestrator pauses pipeline and escalates to human immediately with specific description and suggested fix.
  • HIGH: Logic bug or missing test coverage for core behavior. Orchestrator routes back to IMPLEMENTER for one fix round.
  • MEDIUM: Logic issue or convention violation that will fail CI. Routes back to IMPLEMENTER.
  • LOW: Minor convention issue. Dispatched to TICKET agent as NICE_TO_HAVE follow-up; does not block.

AI transparency: Footer on every posted inline comment: "— This review was generated with AI assistance."

Evolved QA ENGINEER agent subagent isolated context E2E extended

Responsibility: Validates all acceptance criteria using the extended E2E tier. Returns a machine-readable QA report to the orchestrator and posts the full report as a PR/MR comment.

The orchestrator reads the report to decide on loop-back (QA FAIL → one more round with IMPLEMENTER) versus escalation (QA FAIL after loop → human decision with specific failing criteria listed).

The extended E2E tier covers: full acceptance criteria, regression, visual comparison, edge cases, and the test authoring obligation — every manually validated flow without an existing automated test gets one written and committed before the QA report is finalized.

Feedback items in the QA report are classified with the same MoSCoW tiers. COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE recommendations are dispatched to the TICKET agent by the orchestrator as non-blocking follow-up tasks.

AI transparency: QA comments posted to GitHub/GitLab carry an AI-generated notice in the footer.

INVOKE CHALLENGER
Grooming output: effort: "M", risk_level: "MEDIUM", complexity: "MEDIUM", risk_notes: "Three approach options considered. Selected transient-based storage, but the concurrency behavior under WordPress multisite is unclear. Medium confidence."
Decision: Invoke. MEDIUM risk alone triggers CHALLENGER. Additionally, risk_notes reveals an open unknown about multisite behavior — exactly the kind of hidden assumption CHALLENGER is built to surface.
INVOKE CHALLENGER
Grooming output: effort: "L", risk_level: "LOW", complexity: "LOW", risk_notes: "Large refactor but purely mechanical. All changes follow the same pattern."
Decision: Invoke. L effort triggers CHALLENGER regardless of risk level. Even mechanical refactors at this scale benefit from adversarial review — blast radius on failure is high.
INVOKE CHALLENGER
Grooming output: effort: "S", risk_level: "LOW", complexity: "LOW", risk_notes: "Small change, but it touches the authentication middleware. Behavior under concurrent sessions was not verified during exploration."
Decision: Invoke. Structured fields say skip, but risk_notes surfaces an auth-adjacent unknown. Authentication changes get CHALLENGER regardless of effort size.
SKIP CHALLENGER
Grooming output: effort: "S", risk_level: "MEDIUM", complexity: "LOW", risk_notes: "Risk is MEDIUM because the feature is user-facing. But the change is a simple label update with no logic involved. Very high confidence."
Decision: Skip. MEDIUM risk normally triggers, but risk_notes clarifies the risk source is cosmetic, not logic. The orchestrator can use judgment to skip CHALLENGER for user-facing label changes with zero logic risk.

8. Runtime scenarios

Three concrete runs that illustrate how the pipeline behaves end to end. Each scenario narrates the orchestrator's decisions at every routing point, shows how agents communicate, and highlights the design choices that govern that class of ticket.

Scenario A — Simple bug fix (cache TTL miscalculation)

Input: "Cache TTL is off by a factor of 60. The conversion from minutes to seconds is missing in src/Cache/Manager.php:142."

  1. TICKET agent — Produces 01-ticket: one-line description, file identified, zero acceptance tests (trivial fix), label bug.
  2. GROOMING agent — Reads Manager.php and its callers. Returns: effort: "XS", risk_level: "LOW", complexity: "LOW", risk_notes: "Single arithmetic correction. No callers pass a pre-multiplied value. High confidence."
  3. Pipeline configuration — Orchestrator reads grooming output. Applies rules: XS + LOW → skip CHALLENGER; no public API change → skip DOCS; XS → QA smoke-only. PR REVIEWER always runs. Pipeline: IMPLEMENTER → DOD gate → PR REVIEWER → QA (smoke).
  4. IMPLEMENTER — Applies the multiplication fix. Runs DOCS (no-op, no API change), DOD (pass: lint clean, existing tests pass), PR OPENER (opens PR with Co-Authored-By: Claude and AI-generated notice). Returns 03-implementation.
  5. Orchestrator DOD gate — Invokes DOD skill independently. Result: PASS. Proceeds.
  6. PR REVIEWER — Posts inline comment confirming fix is correct. No blockers. Returns verdict: "APPROVED", comments_posted: true.
  7. QA ENGINEER (smoke) — Runs smoke tests. Returns PASS. Pipeline completes.

Total agents invoked: TICKET, GROOMING, IMPLEMENTER, PR REVIEWER, QA. CHALLENGER and deep QA skipped. Entry-level routing eliminated four agent calls compared to the maximum path.

Scenario B — Feature addition (user notification preferences)

Input: "Users should be able to opt out of transactional email notifications per category (marketing, billing, security). Preferences persist per account."

  1. TICKET agent — Produces 01-ticket: structured acceptance criteria (preference UI, persistence, email send logic respects preferences), labels feature, user-facing.
  2. GROOMING agent — Explores notification send path, account model, and UI component patterns. Returns: effort: "M", risk_level: "MEDIUM", complexity: "MEDIUM", risk_notes: "User-facing preference changes. The notification send path has three callers; all need to be gated. Medium confidence — the billing notification exemption from opt-out (security/legal requirement) was inferred but not confirmed in the codebase."
  3. Pipeline configuration — Orchestrator reads grooming output. M effort + MEDIUM risk + user-facing + unresolved billing exemption → invoke CHALLENGER. Public API change (new preferences endpoint) → run DOCS. M effort → full QA depth. Pipeline: CHALLENGER → IMPLEMENTER → DOCS → DOD gate → PR REVIEWER → QA.
  4. CHALLENGER — Reviews the plan. Confirms the billing notification exemption gap. Returns verdict: "NEEDS_REVISION", feedback: one MUST_HAVE item (billing/security notifications must always send regardless of preference, legal requirement), one COULD_HAVE (consider preference inheritance for sub-accounts). Loop count: 0.
  5. Orchestrator routes back to GROOMING — MUST_HAVE revision required. GROOMING revises: adds explicit billing/security opt-out exemption to the plan. Returns updated grooming output.
  6. CHALLENGER (second pass) — Reviews updated plan. Returns verdict: "APPROVED".
  7. Orchestrator dispatches NTH — COULD_HAVE sub-account inheritance item → TICKET agent invoked in parallel, non-blocking, to file a follow-up issue. Pipeline continues without waiting.
  8. IMPLEMENTER — Implements preferences schema, UI, and gated send path with billing exemption. Runs DOCS (new API endpoint documented), DOD (pass), PR OPENER. Returns 03-implementation.
  9. Orchestrator DOD gate — PASS. Proceeds.
  10. PR REVIEWER — Posts inline comments. One SHOULD_HAVE: missing index on preferences table. Returns verdict: "APPROVED" (no blockers), comments_posted: true.
  11. Orchestrator dispatches NTH — SHOULD_HAVE missing index → TICKET agent invoked in parallel to file follow-up issue.
  12. QA ENGINEER — Full depth. Runs integration and E2E tests. PASS. Pipeline completes.

Total agents invoked: Full pipeline. CHALLENGER invoked twice (one revision loop). Two follow-up issues filed non-blocking. GROOMING iteration resolved a legal requirement gap before implementation began.

Scenario C — Architectural blocker (missing data model)

Input: "Implement multi-tenant support so enterprise accounts can have isolated data namespaces."

  1. TICKET agent — Produces 01-ticket: high-level acceptance criteria, labels feature, architectural, breaking-change.
  2. GROOMING agent — Explores the data layer, account model, and query patterns. Returns: effort: "XL", risk_level: "HIGH", complexity: "HIGH", risk_notes: "No tenant isolation primitives exist anywhere in the codebase. Every table uses a flat account_id. The approach — row-level scoping vs. separate schema per tenant — is an irreversible architectural decision. Plan assumes row-level scoping but this was not validated against the account volume projections."
  3. Pipeline configuration — XL + HIGH + architectural + breaking change → CHALLENGER always; full QA. Pipeline: CHALLENGER → IMPLEMENTER → DOCS → DOD gate → PR REVIEWER → QA.
  4. CHALLENGER — Reviews the plan. The row-level scoping assumption is unvalidated and irreversible. Returns verdict: "BLOCKED": no tenant isolation data model exists; row-level vs. separate-schema decision cannot be made from the codebase alone. alternative_suggestions: ["(A) Row-level scoping: add tenant_id column to all tables + row-level security policies. Lower migration cost, higher query complexity. Works if account volume stays below ~10k tenants.", "(B) Separate schema per tenant: full isolation, higher ops overhead, requires dynamic schema management. Correct choice if regulatory isolation is required."]. Loop count: 0.
  5. Orchestrator routes back to GROOMING — Loop count 0, one iteration allowed. Orchestrator passes the CHALLENGER's BLOCKED reason and alternative_suggestions to GROOMING: "Revise the plan. The tenant isolation approach is unvalidated. Evaluate both alternatives against what is known from the codebase and flag explicitly what cannot be determined without human input."
  6. GROOMING (revision) — Re-examines the codebase with the two alternatives in scope. Produces a revised plan: documents the structural fit of each option, identifies three queries that would need major rewrite under option B, confirms no regulatory isolation requirement is present in the codebase. Returns updated grooming output with risk_notes: "Both options are technically viable. Option A is lower risk given current scale. Option B would be the right choice if regulatory isolation is later required — this is the only decision the codebase cannot answer. High confidence on Option A; human call needed only to confirm regulatory stance."
  7. CHALLENGER (second pass) — Reviews revised plan. The regulatory question is still genuinely open and irreversible. Returns verdict: "BLOCKED" again. Loop count: 1. alternative_suggestions: ["Proceed with Option A (row-level scoping) with an explicit architecture decision record (ADR) committing to this approach. If regulatory isolation is later required, plan a full migration. This is the only path that does not require blocking the feature on a policy decision that engineering cannot make."]
  8. Orchestrator escalates to human — Loop count ≥ 1. Escalation message contains: (1) Blocker: The row-level vs. separate-schema decision is irreversible and depends on regulatory isolation requirements not present in the codebase. (2) Proposed path forward: Option A (row-level scoping) is viable at current scale. CHALLENGER suggests proceeding with an ADR if regulatory isolation is not required. (3) Why human judgment is needed: Engineering cannot determine the regulatory isolation requirement from the codebase. This is a product/legal decision that sets an irreversible architectural direction. Human input needed on: is regulatory data isolation required for enterprise accounts?

Total agents invoked: TICKET, GROOMING (×2), CHALLENGER (×2), then human escalation. The escalation message is actionable: the human receives a specific binary question backed by two analyzed alternatives, not a vague request to "design something first."

9. AI transparency policy

Every artifact produced by the pipeline carries a visible record of AI involvement. This is not optional and has no team-level opt-out.

Commit attribution

Every commit on an AI-generated branch carries:

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

This applies to every commit the IMPLEMENTER creates, including fixup commits from DOD self-correction. The trailer is added automatically by the IMPLEMENTER during git operations.

Issue and PR descriptions

Every issue created by the TICKET agent and every PR opened by the PR OPENER skill carries a visible notice at the top of the description:

⚠️ AI-generated — created by an automated pipeline. Review before acting on this.

This appears before any other content in the body so it is visible without scrolling.

Review comments

Every inline review comment posted by the PR REVIEWER carries an AI-generated footer identifying the comment as automated output.

AGENTS.md

Every repository using the pipeline must include an AGENTS.md file at the root. This file is the cross-tool authority for AI agent behavior in the repository. It documents: which agents are permitted to operate, what branches they may push to, what commands they may run, and any repository-specific constraints on tool use. All agents read AGENTS.md at the start of their context before taking any action.

10. Standard skills

Skills are reusable, composable units of behavior that agents invoke. They run in the invoking agent's context. The following skills are part of the standard pipeline distribution.

DOD skill

Runs the Definition of Done checklist for the current branch. Checks: lint, test suite, build, coverage threshold, commit message format, AGENTS.md present. Returns a structured result with overall: "PASS" | "WARN" | "FAIL" and a per-check breakdown. Used by the IMPLEMENTER (Layer 1 self-correction) and by the orchestrator (Layer 2 independent gate).

WARN items are surfaced to the human but do not block the pipeline. FAIL items block forward progress. The IMPLEMENTER self-corrects FAIL items before handing off; if the orchestrator's gate also returns FAIL after one loop-back, it escalates to human.

DOCS skill

Updates developer-facing documentation to reflect changes on the current branch. Reads the diff, identifies public API changes, and rewrites or creates the affected documentation sections. Invoked by the IMPLEMENTER after implementation and before DOD. No-op if grooming flagged no public API changes.

PR OPENER skill

Opens a pull request for the current branch. Fills all sections of the PR template from the ticket, grooming output, and implementation summary. Adds the AI-generated notice at the top of the PR description. Adds Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com> to the PR metadata. Invoked by the IMPLEMENTER after DOD passes.

E2E skill

Provides end-to-end test execution at two tiers:

  • Basic tier — Used by GROOMING (pre-implementation smoke check to establish a baseline) and by the IMPLEMENTER (post-implementation smoke check). Runs a limited suite against the current branch. Fast enough to fit inside an agent's execution window.
  • Extended tier — Used by the QA ENGINEER. Full E2E suite with scenario coverage matching the acceptance criteria in the ticket. Writes new E2E tests when coverage gaps are identified.

Screenshots captured during E2E runs are posted as comments to the issue or PR on GitHub or GitLab, but not stored in the repository.

The v3 design proposal both incorporates lessons from these systems and introduces evolutions based on 2026 research on multi-agent coordination. The orchestrator in v3 isn't a fixed sequence—it reads the grooming output and makes all routing decisions dynamically from there. This means the log becomes a living document of the orchestrator's decision-making process rather than a predetermined template.

For the redesign itself, I'm shifting away from hardcoded pipeline steps entirely. Instead, the orchestrator reads the grooming JSON, makes conditional routing calls transparently, and each agent returns structured JSON that feeds back into the next routing decision. The log will show this as a "Routing decisions" section that grows dynamically, with agent invocations listed in the order they were actually called, each entry explaining the orchestrator's reasoning and the agent's output summary.

---
name: release-agent
description: Handles pushing the branch to remote and creating the GitHub pull request. Invoked by the orchestrator after lead-reviewer returns PASS. Does not write code or modify files other than filling the PR draft.
tools: [Bash, Read, Write]
---

# Release Agent

You push the branch to remote and create the GitHub pull request. You do not write code. You do not modify implementation files.

## Inputs
- Issue number `N`
- Branch name
- Base branch
- Acceptance criteria list (for the PR body)
- Spec path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/issues/<N>-spec.md`)

---

## Process

### Step 1 — Push
```bash
git push -u origin <branch>
```

### Step 2 — Initialize PR draft
```bash
bash .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/scripts/init-pr-draft.sh <N>
```

This creates `.TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/pull/<N>.md` from the template.

### Step 3 — Fill the PR draft
Read the spec and the initialized draft. Fill **every section** — no placeholder text left behind.

- Title line in the draft: `Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>`
  **Never** use conventional commit prefix format (`fix(xxx):`, `feat(xxx):`, etc.) in the PR title — that format is for git commits only.
- "What was done": summarize the implementation from the spec
- "How to test": derive from the acceptance criteria
- "Type of change": select exactly one checkbox matching the change type
- Leave "What was tested" blank — the orchestrator fills it after QA

### Step 4 — Create the PR
```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "Closes #<N>: <short descriptive title>" \
  --body "$(cat .TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/pull/<N>.md)" \
  --base <base_branch> \
  --draft
```

Then assign and label:
```bash
gh pr edit <PR_number> --add-assignee @me --add-label "Made by AI"
```
(Skip the label silently if it does not exist in the repo.)

---

## Return

Report:
- PR number
- PR URL
- Branch pushed: yes/no
- Any errors encountered

1. Current state: what we have

114 115
116 The gas-delivery-pipeline-templates plugin is a working linear pipeline driven by a single orchestrator skill. It covers the full engineering lifecycle from raw description to QA validation. The system works well. The question is not whether to replace it, but how to make it genuinely agentic — moving from a chain of sequential skills to an adaptive, self-routing network of specialized agents. 117
118 119

The current pipeline runs in a fixed linear sequence:

120 121
122 153
154 155

The pipeline is strong but has two structural limitations. First, the orchestrator is reactive, not adaptive: it follows a fixed sequence with manual pause points rather than routing dynamically based on what each agent produces. Second, the quality gates (grooming, review-pr) have no feedback loops — when grooming identifies a high-risk plan, there is no mechanism to challenge it before handing off to implementation.

2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership

171 172
173 The following is a structured extraction from raw notes, organized by theme. These ideas form the basis of the new design. 174
175 176

Architecture shift

177

Move from a single orchestrator skill with inline stages to a true orchestrator-and-subagents pattern. The orchestrator owns coordination logic and routing decisions. Every stage runs as an isolated subagent with a clean context window. This eliminates context rot, reduces cross-contamination between phases, and makes each agent unit-testable.

178 179

Grooming gets an adversary

180

The current grooming skill self-challenges its own output. That is insufficient for complex or high-risk changes. A dedicated CHALLENGER agent — a skeptical senior engineer — should independently review the grooming plan, looking for hidden assumptions, missing risks, and reasons not to proceed. This agent should not be invoked for every ticket: the orchestrator decides based on the complexity and risk level returned by the GROOMING agent. Trivial fixes skip it entirely. Complex or high-risk plans always go through it, with up to two rounds of back-and-forth before escalating to a human.

181 182

End-to-end testing as a shared primitive

183

End-to-end capability (Playwright for UI, curl/API calls for backends) should not live exclusively in the QA agent. The IMPLEMENTER needs basic E2E validation to confirm its own work before handing off. The GROOMING agent may also use the basic E2E tier to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration. The recommendation: define E2E as a shared skill that multiple agents can access at a basic level, with the QA ENGINEER using an extended version that goes deeper into edge cases, regression scenarios, and visual comparison.

184 185

Context discipline in the orchestrator

186

Every agent invocation must receive exactly the context it needs, no more. The orchestrator is responsible for distilling prior outputs into the minimal structured handoff for each downstream agent. A CHALLENGER needs the ticket and the grooming plan — not the full interaction history leading up to it. A PR REVIEWER only needs the diff, ticket, and conventions — not the grooming discussion. The orchestrator acts as a context editor, not a context relay.

187 188

Structured return contracts

189

Every agent must return a machine-readable structured object (JSON) directly to the orchestrator. The orchestrator receives the return value, makes a routing decision, and passes only the relevant fields to the next agent. Each agent's contract is defined by its output schema: specific fields, specific value ranges, specific verdict flags. Natural language is for human-facing summaries only — the routing logic runs on the structured part.

190

Agents that produce reviews, challenges, or assessments classify each feedback item with a priority tier: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional enhancement). The orchestrator uses this classification to route: MUST_HAVE items drive loop-back or escalation logic; SHOULD_HAVE and below items that are not blocking are dispatched to the TICKET agent as parallel, non-blocking follow-up tasks. The main pipeline does not wait for these secondary tasks.

191 192

Risk-based routing

193

The orchestrator adjusts the pipeline dynamically based on what it learns at each stage. All routing decisions happen after the GROOMING agent returns, never before. Key routing signals: effort size (XL → always invoke CHALLENGER), risk level from GROOMING (HIGH → always invoke CHALLENGER), blocker criticality from PR REVIEWER (CRITICAL → pause for human, HIGH → loop to implementer), QA result (FAIL → loop to implementer before escalating).

194 195

Loop-back protocols

196

Feedback loops should be first-class pipeline primitives, not manual workarounds. GROOMING ↔ CHALLENGER loops (max 2 rounds for NEEDS_REVISION, 1 round for BLOCKED), IMPLEMENTER ↔ PR REVIEWER loops (max 1 round per blocker criticality tier), and IMPLEMENTER ↔ QA ENGINEER loops are modelled explicitly in the orchestrator's logic with round counters and escalation conditions.

197 198

Continuous updates of Git tools

199

Agents must report their work just like humans do on GitHub or GitLab: issues, comments for grooming, pull requests, etc. Each agent is responsible for handling its own Git operations. The orchestrator can route nice to havs and feedback for later to the ticket writer so they are stored in the backlog, without stopping the main flow.

200 201

AI transparency

202

All AI-generated content written to external systems (GitHub issues, GitLab tickets, PR descriptions, MR descriptions) must carry a clearly visible AI-generated notice. All commits must include a Co-Authored-By tag. This applies to everything the pipeline writes, without exception, and is enforced by the agents themselves.

203 204

Generic + customizable

205

The pipeline ships as a reusable template that any team can adopt out of the box. The only component that should be team-specific is the IMPLEMENTER agent, which needs to know the codebase conventions, tech stack, test commands, and team patterns. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend and backend, for instance — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents. All other agents work generically without customization.

206 207

3. State of the art: what the field has learned

208 209
210 Several converging findings from 2025–2026 production agentic systems directly inform this design. The key insight: architecture matters more than model choice. The gap between a 10% productivity improvement and a 25–30% improvement is not model capability — it is context engineering. 211
212 213

Context rot is real and architectural

214

Chroma Research (2025) demonstrated that LLM performance degrades consistently as input tokens increase, even on simple tasks, and degrades faster on multi-step reasoning. This is context rot. It means a single agent that accumulates the full history of an exploration session, planning debates, and test failures will produce worse output at the PR review stage than a fresh agent given only the relevant context. The solution is architectural: subagent isolation, not larger context windows.

215

A correlated finding: agents miss relevant context 56% of the time when relying on on-demand retrieval. This makes explicit structured handoffs — where the orchestrator packages exactly what each agent needs — far more reliable than letting agents fetch their own context from conversation history.

216 217

The adversarial review pattern reduces errors and cost

218

Production systems (notably Hugues Clouâtre's architecture, deployed across multiple Rust projects) use a SCOUT + GUARD pattern: an exploratory agent produces a research report, and a smaller adversarial agent stress-tests it before a planner synthesizes both. Finding flaws in a concrete proposal requires less reasoning range than producing one — which means a smaller, cheaper model can handle adversarial review effectively. This is why the CHALLENGER agent in this design can be a smaller model, while the GROOMING agent must be a capable one.

219 220

Structured JSON return contracts are the coordination layer

221

The field has converged on typed JSON as the communication protocol between agents. Agents return structured objects directly to the orchestrator rather than persisting files or sharing conversation history. Three practical reasons: the contracts are auditable (every decision is recorded in the orchestrator's context), resumable (any session can be restarted from a checkpoint), and debuggable (failures include exact locations and actionable next steps). This design defines a typed JSON schema for every agent's output, passed as a return value through the orchestrator.

222 223

Unstructured multi-agent networks amplify errors

224

Research on multi-agent LLM pipelines found that unstructured networks amplify errors up to 17.2× compared to single-agent baselines. When agents are chained without explicit topology and structured communication contracts, each agent's output noise becomes the next agent's input noise. Every agent-to-agent interaction in this design must have a typed schema, not natural language.

225 226

Model routing reduces cost without sacrificing quality

227

Using capable models for planning and reasoning-intensive tasks, and faster/cheaper models for execution-intensive tasks, can reduce API costs by 50–60% versus an all-capable-model approach. The GROOMING agent and ORCHESTRATOR need the most reasoning capability. The CHALLENGER, IMPLEMENTER's basic checks, and the DOD checker can route to faster models.

228 229

AGENTS.md as the shared knowledge layer

230

Vercel's evals (2026) showed that a well-written AGENTS.md file achieved 100% pass rate on build, lint, and test tasks where skill-based approaches maxed out at 79%. Every subagent in this system inherits project context through the project instructions file — not through an explicit handoff every time. This is the "CSS for agents" pattern: global rules cascade into every subagent automatically.

231 232

2026 focus: harnesses, not just agents

233

The engineering emphasis in 2026 has shifted from building individual agents to building the environments, verification loops, and supervision layers that make agents reliable at scale. The orchestrator in this design is the harness: its job is supervision, routing, loop management, and escalation — not execution. Execution is fully delegated to isolated agents.

236 237
238 The new system replaces the linear skill chain with a fully agentic orchestrator-and-subagents architecture. The orchestrator is the only persistent context. All stages run as isolated agents that receive a structured input and return a structured output. The orchestrator reads the output, makes a routing decision, and invokes the next agent — or loops back, or escalates. Two agents always run: TICKET and GROOMING. All other agents are conditional based on what GROOMING returns. 239

Key architectural decisions

The orchestrator owns routing, not execution. The orchestrator's only job is to read structured return values from agents, make routing decisions, and invoke the next agent with the right minimal context. It never runs code, writes files, or produces content itself.
