Internal design document · Engineering AI Systems

Agentic Delivery Pipeline v2.1

Prepared May 2026 · Based on gas-delivery-pipeline-templates plugin + state-of-the-art research

Contents

  1. Current state: what we have
  2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership
  3. State of the art: what the field has learned
  4. New system design
  5. Agent catalog: responsibilities & contracts
  6. Agent communication schemas
  7. Orchestrator routing logic
  8. Runtime scenarios
  9. AI transparency policy
  10. Standard skills: duplication detection & E2E
  11. Comparison with current systems (WP Rocket, Imagify, BackWPUp)

1. Current state: what we have

The gas-delivery-pipeline-templates plugin is a working linear pipeline driven by a single orchestrator skill. It covers the full engineering lifecycle from raw description to QA validation. The system works well. The question is not whether to replace it, but how to make it genuinely agentic — moving from a chain of sequential skills to an adaptive, self-routing network of specialized agents.

The current pipeline runs in a fixed linear sequence:

The pipeline is strong but has two structural limitations. First, the orchestrator is reactive, not adaptive: it follows a fixed sequence with manual pause points rather than routing dynamically based on what each agent produces. Second, the quality gates (grooming, review-pr) have no feedback loops — when grooming identifies a high-risk plan, there is no mechanism to challenge it before handing off to implementation.

ComponentCurrent formLimitation
delivery-orchestrationSkill (inline, linear)No adaptive routing, no risk-based branching
ticket-writerSkill (inline)No structured JSON output for downstream agents
groomingSkill (inline, single-pass)No codebase exploration phase, no adversarial review, no challenger agent
implementationMain agent (same context)No E2E capability, no self-run DOD check, not isolated
technical-documentationSkill (inline)Fine as-is
dodSkill (inline, orchestrator-run)Output is prose, not machine-readable; single layer only
open-prSkill (inline)No AI transparency annotation
review-prSubagent (isolated)No criticality tiers, no inline comment posting, no loop-back protocol
qa-engineerSubagent (isolated)No shared E2E primitive, Playwright only in QA, no test authoring obligation

2. Structured ideas from engineering leadership

The following is a structured extraction from raw notes, organized by theme. These ideas form the basis of the new design.

Architecture shift

Move from a single orchestrator skill with inline stages to a true orchestrator-and-subagents pattern. The orchestrator owns coordination logic and routing decisions. Every stage runs as an isolated subagent with a clean context window. This eliminates context rot, reduces cross-contamination between phases, and makes each agent unit-testable.

Grooming gets an adversary

The current grooming skill self-challenges its own output. That is insufficient for complex or high-risk changes. A dedicated CHALLENGER agent — a skeptical senior engineer — should independently review the grooming plan, looking for hidden assumptions, missing risks, and reasons not to proceed. This agent should not be invoked for every ticket: the orchestrator decides based on the complexity and risk level returned by the GROOMING agent. Trivial fixes skip it entirely. Complex or high-risk plans always go through it, with up to two rounds of back-and-forth before escalating to a human.

End-to-end testing as a shared primitive

End-to-end capability (Playwright for UI, curl/API calls for backends) should not live exclusively in the QA agent. The IMPLEMENTER needs basic E2E validation to confirm its own work before handing off. The GROOMING agent may also use the basic E2E tier to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration. The recommendation: define E2E as a shared skill that multiple agents can access at a basic level, with the QA ENGINEER using an extended version that goes deeper into edge cases, regression scenarios, and visual comparison.

Context discipline in the orchestrator

Every agent invocation must receive exactly the context it needs, no more. The orchestrator is responsible for distilling prior outputs into the minimal structured handoff for each downstream agent. A CHALLENGER needs the ticket and the grooming plan — not the full interaction history leading up to it. A PR REVIEWER only needs the diff, ticket, and conventions — not the grooming discussion. The orchestrator acts as a context editor, not a context relay.

Structured return contracts

Every agent must return a machine-readable structured object (JSON) directly to the orchestrator. The orchestrator receives the return value, makes a routing decision, and passes only the relevant fields to the next agent. Each agent's contract is defined by its output schema: specific fields, specific value ranges, specific verdict flags. Natural language is for human-facing summaries only — the routing logic runs on the structured part.

Agents that produce reviews, challenges, or assessments classify each feedback item with a priority tier: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional enhancement). The orchestrator uses this classification to route: MUST_HAVE items drive loop-back or escalation logic; SHOULD_HAVE and below items that are not blocking are dispatched to the TICKET agent as parallel, non-blocking follow-up tasks. The main pipeline does not wait for these secondary tasks.

Risk-based routing

The orchestrator adjusts the pipeline dynamically based on what it learns at each stage. All routing decisions happen after the GROOMING agent returns, never before. Key routing signals: effort size (XL → always invoke CHALLENGER), risk level from GROOMING (HIGH → always invoke CHALLENGER), blocker criticality from PR REVIEWER (CRITICAL → pause for human, HIGH → loop to implementer), QA result (FAIL → loop to implementer before escalating).

Loop-back protocols

Feedback loops should be first-class pipeline primitives, not manual workarounds. GROOMING ↔ CHALLENGER loops (max 2 rounds for NEEDS_REVISION, 1 round for BLOCKED), IMPLEMENTER ↔ PR REVIEWER loops (max 1 round per blocker criticality tier), and IMPLEMENTER ↔ QA ENGINEER loops are modelled explicitly in the orchestrator's logic with round counters and escalation conditions.

Continuous updates of Git tools

Agents must report their work just like humans do on GitHub or GitLab: issues, comments for grooming, pull requests, etc. Each agent is responsible for handling its own Git operations. The orchestrator can route nice to havs and feedback for later to the ticket writer so they are stored in the backlog, without stopping the main flow.

AI transparency

All AI-generated content written to external systems (GitHub issues, GitLab tickets, PR descriptions, MR descriptions) must carry a clearly visible AI-generated notice. All commits must include a Co-Authored-By tag. This applies to everything the pipeline writes, without exception, and is enforced by the agents themselves.

Generic + customizable

The pipeline ships as a reusable template that any team can adopt out of the box. The only component that should be team-specific is the IMPLEMENTER agent, which needs to know the codebase conventions, tech stack, test commands, and team patterns. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend and backend, for instance — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents. All other agents work generically without customization.

3. State of the art: what the field has learned

Several converging findings from 2025–2026 production agentic systems directly inform this design. The key insight: architecture matters more than model choice. The gap between a 10% productivity improvement and a 25–30% improvement is not model capability — it is context engineering.

Context rot is real and architectural

Chroma Research (2025) demonstrated that LLM performance degrades consistently as input tokens increase, even on simple tasks, and degrades faster on multi-step reasoning. This is context rot. It means a single agent that accumulates the full history of an exploration session, planning debates, and test failures will produce worse output at the PR review stage than a fresh agent given only the relevant context. The solution is architectural: subagent isolation, not larger context windows.

A correlated finding: agents miss relevant context 56% of the time when relying on on-demand retrieval. This makes explicit structured handoffs — where the orchestrator packages exactly what each agent needs — far more reliable than letting agents fetch their own context from conversation history.

The adversarial review pattern reduces errors and cost

Production systems (notably Hugues Clouâtre's architecture, deployed across multiple Rust projects) use a SCOUT + GUARD pattern: an exploratory agent produces a research report, and a smaller adversarial agent stress-tests it before a planner synthesizes both. Finding flaws in a concrete proposal requires less reasoning range than producing one — which means a smaller, cheaper model can handle adversarial review effectively. This is why the CHALLENGER agent in this design can be a smaller model, while the GROOMING agent must be a capable one.

Structured JSON return contracts are the coordination layer

The field has converged on typed JSON as the communication protocol between agents. Agents return structured objects directly to the orchestrator rather than persisting files or sharing conversation history. Three practical reasons: the contracts are auditable (every decision is recorded in the orchestrator's context), resumable (any session can be restarted from a checkpoint), and debuggable (failures include exact locations and actionable next steps). This design defines a typed JSON schema for every agent's output, passed as a return value through the orchestrator.

Unstructured multi-agent networks amplify errors

Research on multi-agent LLM pipelines found that unstructured networks amplify errors up to 17.2× compared to single-agent baselines. When agents are chained without explicit topology and structured communication contracts, each agent's output noise becomes the next agent's input noise. Every agent-to-agent interaction in this design must have a typed schema, not natural language.

Model routing reduces cost without sacrificing quality

Using capable models for planning and reasoning-intensive tasks, and faster/cheaper models for execution-intensive tasks, can reduce API costs by 50–60% versus an all-capable-model approach. The GROOMING agent and ORCHESTRATOR need the most reasoning capability. The CHALLENGER, IMPLEMENTER's basic checks, and the DOD checker can route to faster models.

AGENTS.md as the shared knowledge layer

Vercel's evals (2026) showed that a well-written AGENTS.md file achieved 100% pass rate on build, lint, and test tasks where skill-based approaches maxed out at 79%. Every subagent in this system inherits project context through the project instructions file — not through an explicit handoff every time. This is the "CSS for agents" pattern: global rules cascade into every subagent automatically.

2026 focus: harnesses, not just agents

The engineering emphasis in 2026 has shifted from building individual agents to building the environments, verification loops, and supervision layers that make agents reliable at scale. The orchestrator in this design is the harness: its job is supervision, routing, loop management, and escalation — not execution. Execution is fully delegated to isolated agents.

4. New system design

The new system replaces the linear skill chain with a fully agentic orchestrator-and-subagents architecture. The orchestrator is the only persistent context. All stages run as isolated agents that receive a structured input and return a structured output. The orchestrator reads the output, makes a routing decision, and invokes the next agent — or loops back, or escalates. Two agents always run: TICKET and GROOMING. All other agents are conditional based on what GROOMING returns.

System overview

Key architectural decisions

The orchestrator owns routing, not execution. The orchestrator's only job is to read structured return values from agents, make routing decisions, and invoke the next agent with the right minimal context. It never runs code, writes files, or produces content itself.

TICKET and GROOMING always run. These are the two mandatory stages in every pipeline run. All other routing decisions — whether to invoke CHALLENGER, PR REVIEWER, dedicated QA, or DOCS — are made post-grooming using grooming.risk_level, grooming.effort, and the grooming.risk_notes prose field. Nothing is routed before the grooming output is available.

DOCS, DOD, and PR OPENER are IMPLEMENTER skills, not orchestrator-dispatched agents. The IMPLEMENTER runs these as inline steps before handing off. It updates docs, runs a first DOD check (layer 1) and self-corrects any issues it can resolve, then opens the PR. The orchestrator runs a second independent DOD gate (layer 2) before invoking the PR REVIEWER. This two-layer approach catches issues the IMPLEMENTER missed without requiring a separate agent dispatch for routine work.

Non-blocking NTH dispatch. When any agent returns COULD_HAVE or NICE_TO_HAVE feedback items, the orchestrator dispatches the TICKET agent to create follow-up tickets for those items as a parallel, non-blocking task. The main pipeline continues immediately without waiting.

E2E as a shared primitive. Playwright and API-call capability is available to any agent that needs it via a shared E2E skill. The GROOMING agent and IMPLEMENTER use a basic version (behavioral verification and smoke tests). The QA ENGINEER uses an extended version covering full acceptance criteria, regression, visual comparison, and edge cases.

5. Agent catalog

Each agent is defined by its type (subagent in isolated context, or skill running inline), its required input, its output schema, its routing authority, and its AI transparency obligations. GROOMING combines codebase exploration and planning in a single isolated pass. DOCS, DOD, and PR OPENER run as inline skills inside the IMPLEMENTER.
Orchestrator ORCHESTRATOR persistent context no execution

Responsibility: Receive the initial input, determine pipeline scope, invoke agents in order, evaluate structured return values, route forward or loop back, escalate to human when routing rules are exhausted.

Model: Capable reasoning model (Sonnet-class or above). Temperature: 0.2 — routing decisions should be consistent, not creative.

Does not: Execute code. Write files. Produce content. Generate issues or PRs directly.

Routing authority: All routing decisions happen after GROOMING returns. The orchestrator reads grooming.risk_level, grooming.effort, and grooming.risk_notes to decide whether to invoke CHALLENGER. Decides loop-back based on review.blockers[*].criticality and qa.overall. Runs the independent DOD layer-2 gate after the IMPLEMENTER hands off. Escalates to human when loop counters are exhausted — always with 1–2 concrete next steps sourced from agent output. Dispatches TICKET agent in parallel for any COULD_HAVE or NICE_TO_HAVE feedback items returned by CHALLENGER, PR REVIEWER, or QA ENGINEER. Once the task is completed and the agentic system stops, the orchestrator returns a structured report to the user with links to the issue & PR, conclusions of each reviewer agents (grooming reviewer, pr reviewer, qa), possible gaps & risks, next steps and follow-up tickets created in any. The report is posted on the main ticket on the git tool as well.

Evolved TICKET agent subagent isolated context always runs

Input: Raw description — prompt, Slack thread, Confluence page, URL, verbal notes. Can also receive a structured NTH feedback item from the orchestrator for follow-up ticket creation.

Output: Structured ticket object. Creates the issue in GitHub/GitLab with AI-generated notice.

AI transparency: All created issues include a notice at the top: "⚠️ This issue was generated with AI assistance. Review before acting."

Model: Fast model sufficient. Temperature: 0.3.

Evolved GROOMING agent subagent explore + plan always runs

Responsibility: A single isolated agent that performs codebase exploration and planning in one pass. It reads files freely, iterates between discovery and reasoning, selects an approach, and produces a structured plan with risk assessment. It does not implement anything. The grooming plan is posted as a comment on the ticket or edited if this is an iteration.

Input: Ticket object from TICKET agent + read-only codebase access.

Output: Grooming object — relevant files, chosen approach, development steps, test plan, risks with severity, effort estimate, risk level, risk_notes prose field, and open questions.

Key output fields: risk_level and effort are the primary routing signals the orchestrator uses post-grooming. risk_notes is a short prose field: confidence level, key risks, anything the orchestrator should weight when making conditional routing decisions.

Model: Capable reasoning model. Temperature: 0.4 — exploratory enough to find non-obvious patterns, focused enough for structured output.

Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash (read-only commands). E2E capability (basic tier) — to verify behavioral assumptions about the current system during exploration when needed.

New CHALLENGER agent conditional risk ≥ MEDIUM or effort ≥ L adversarial

Role: A skeptical senior engineer whose only job is to find good reasons not to proceed with the plan as written. Not creative, not constructive — adversarial. Surfaces hidden risks, challenges assumptions, identifies missing steps, proposes alternative approaches. The review is posted as a comment on the ticket or edited if this is an iteration.

Input: Ticket object + grooming output. The ticket provides the original requirement context; the grooming output is what the CHALLENGER reviews. Full interaction history is not passed.

Output: Challenge report — verdict (APPROVED / NEEDS_REVISION / BLOCKED), feedback array with MoSCoW severity classification, and — when verdict is not APPROVED — a required alternative_suggestions array with 1–2 concrete alternatives.

Feedback severity tiers: MUST_HAVE (blocks progress — drives verdict to NEEDS_REVISION or BLOCKED), SHOULD_HAVE (strong recommendation), COULD_HAVE (meaningful improvement), NICE_TO_HAVE (optional). COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE items are dispatched to TICKET agent by the orchestrator as non-blocking follow-up tasks.

Loop protocol: If verdict = NEEDS_REVISION, the orchestrator routes the challenge report back to GROOMING (max 2 rounds). If verdict = BLOCKED, the orchestrator gives GROOMING one revision attempt before escalating to human. All escalations include the challenge report and the alternative_suggestions for human resolution.

Model: Fast model sufficient — finding flaws in a concrete plan is lower-entropy than producing one. Temperature: 0.1 — precise, not creative.

Evolved IMPLEMENTER agent code task team-specific isolated worktree

Responsibility: Isolated code task in a dedicated git worktree that also runs DOCS, DOD (layer 1), and PR OPENER as inline skills before handing off.

Input: Grooming output + ticket object + project instructions (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md).

Internal skill sequence:

  1. Implement the plan from the grooming output. Run unit and integration tests — fix until passing.
  2. Run E2E smoke test (basic tier) — confirm the primary happy path works.
  3. Run DOCS skill — update documentation if public API or configuration changed.
  4. Run DOD skill (layer 1) — evaluate the Definition of Done. If any check FAILs: self-correct and re-run until PASS or WARN.
  5. Run PR OPENER skill — open the PR with AI-generated notice. Add Co-Authored-By to all commits.

Output: Implementation report — branch name, files changed, test results, E2E smoke result, DOD layer-1 result, PR URL.

Sub-agent decomposition: The GAS template ships as a single generic IMPLEMENTER. For teams with distinct workstreams — frontend, backend, infrastructure — the IMPLEMENTER can be decomposed into multiple specialized sub-agents that operate in sequence or in parallel. Each sub-agent follows the same internal skill sequence; the orchestrator treats the combined output as a single implementation report. The WordPress teams at group.one use this pattern.

Team-specific: This is the one agent teams should customize. Each team adds their tech stack, test commands, coding conventions, and linting rules to the project instructions.

AI transparency: All commits must include Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>. Usage of AI must be identified in the PR description. Enforced in the agent's instructions and skills.

New E2E CAPABILITY shared skill not a standalone agent

Basic tier (GROOMING + IMPLEMENTER): Start the dev server. Navigate to the main page. Confirm the feature or current behavior works for the primary happy path. Report PASS/FAIL. This is a behavioral verification or sanity check, not full QA.

Extended tier (QA ENGINEER): Full acceptance criteria validation. Regression testing. Edge cases. Visual comparison against design specs. API validation with error paths. Test authoring: any manually validated flow that lacks an automated test must get one — written, run, and committed before the QA report is finalized.

Shared primitive: Both tiers use Playwright MCP + curl. The difference is scope and depth, not tooling. The skill definition includes depth-level parameters.

Evolved DOD — two-layer gate layer 1: IMPLEMENTER skill (self-correcting) layer 2: orchestrator gate (independent)

Layer 1 (IMPLEMENTER): The IMPLEMENTER runs the DOD skill as step 4 in its internal sequence. If any check fails, the IMPLEMENTER self-corrects — fixing missing tests, updating docs, resolving lint errors — and re-runs before handing off.

Layer 2 (orchestrator): The orchestrator runs a second, independent DOD check after receiving the IMPLEMENTER's handoff. It reads the same checks from a fresh perspective, without the IMPLEMENTER's self-correction bias. overall: FAIL at layer 2 routes back to IMPLEMENTER once (max one loop-back); if it fails again, escalate to human with specific blockers.

Why two layers: Self-correction in context introduces bias — the IMPLEMENTER may be blind to patterns it just created. The orchestrator's independent check catches what the IMPLEMENTER normalized.

Evolved DOCS · PR OPENER IMPLEMENTER inline skills

DOCS: Runs inside the IMPLEMENTER as step 3. Receives the explicit list of changed files from the implementation context rather than inferring from git. Updates only files referenced in the grooming output as touched.

PR OPENER: Runs inside the IMPLEMENTER as step 5, after DOD layer 1 passes. Enforces AI transparency: every PR/MR description includes a clearly visible AI-generated notice at the top. All commits on the branch carry the Co-Authored-By tag. Both are unconditional.

Evolved PR REVIEWER agent subagent isolated context

Responsibility: Reviews the PR diff against the ticket and project conventions. Posts inline comments directly to the PR/MR on GitHub/GitLab, then returns a structured review object to the orchestrator.

Inline comment posting is required, not optional. For each blocker and each nice-to-have with a concrete suggestion, the agent posts an inline comment on the relevant file+line. The structured return value is produced in parallel. Both happen before the agent reports complete.

Criticality tiers:

  • CRITICAL: Security vulnerability or breaking change. Orchestrator pauses pipeline and escalates to human immediately with specific description and suggested fix.
  • HIGH: Logic bug or missing test coverage for core behavior. Orchestrator routes back to IMPLEMENTER for one fix round.
  • MEDIUM: Logic issue or convention violation that will fail CI. Routes back to IMPLEMENTER.
  • LOW: Minor convention issue. Dispatched to TICKET agent as NICE_TO_HAVE follow-up; does not block.

AI transparency: Footer on every posted inline comment: "— This review was generated with AI assistance."

Evolved QA ENGINEER agent subagent isolated context E2E extended

Responsibility: Validates all acceptance criteria using the extended E2E tier. Returns a machine-readable QA report to the orchestrator and posts the full report as a PR/MR comment.

The orchestrator reads the report to decide on loop-back (QA FAIL → one more round with IMPLEMENTER) versus escalation (QA FAIL after loop → human decision with specific failing criteria listed).

The extended E2E tier covers: full acceptance criteria, regression, visual comparison, edge cases, and the test authoring obligation — every manually validated flow without an existing automated test gets one written and committed before the QA report is finalized.

Feedback items in the QA report are classified with the same MoSCoW tiers. COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE recommendations are dispatched to the TICKET agent by the orchestrator as non-blocking follow-up tasks.

AI transparency: QA comments posted to GitHub/GitLab carry an AI-generated notice in the footer.

6. Agent communication schemas

Agents communicate by returning typed JSON objects directly to the orchestrator. The orchestrator receives each agent's output in its context, makes a routing decision, and passes only the relevant fields to the next agent — acting as a context editor, not a context relay. Agents never communicate directly; the orchestrator is always the intermediary. The schemas below define the data contract for each agent's output.

Schema definitions

Ticket (TICKET agent output)

{
  "ticket_id": "string",               // GitHub/GitLab issue number
  "ticket_url": "string",
  "title": "string",
  "type": "user_story|bug|chore|epic",
  "description": "string",             // Full content of the ticket, as markdown, including context, expected behavior, acceptance criteria, dependencies and additional notes if any
  "labels": ["string"],
  "sub_tickets": ["string"],          // Populated if this is an EPIC
  "ticket_created": true ,          // True if the ticket was successfully posted on GitHub or GitLab
}

Grooming (GROOMING agent output)

{
  "ticket_id": "string",
  "relevant_files": [
    { "path": "string", "reason": "string" }
  ],
  "approach": "string",               // Chosen approach and rationale
  "development_steps": [
    { "step": "string", "files": ["string"] }
  ],
  "test_plan": "string",
  "risks": [
    {
      "description": "string",
      "severity": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
      "mitigation": "string"
    }
  ],
  "effort": "XS|S|M|L|XL",
  "complexity": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
  "risk_level": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",      // Primary routing signal
  "risk_notes": "string",              // Prose: confidence level, key concerns for orchestrator routing
  "grooming_confidence": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH",
  "open_questions": ["string"]         // Unresolved items requiring human input
  "comment_posted": true           // True if the comment was successfully posted on GitHub or GitLab
}

Challenge (CHALLENGER agent output)

{
  "plan_version": 1,                   // Increments on each revision cycle
  "verdict": "APPROVED|NEEDS_REVISION|BLOCKED",
  "feedback": [
    {
      "description": "string",
      "severity": "MUST_HAVE|SHOULD_HAVE|COULD_HAVE|NICE_TO_HAVE",
      "suggestion": "string"
    }
  ],
  "alternative_suggestions": ["string"],  // REQUIRED when verdict != APPROVED; 1-2 concrete alternatives
  "revised_risk_level": "LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH"
  "comment_posted": true           // True if the comment was successfully posted on GitHub or GitLab
}

Implementation (IMPLEMENTER output)

{
  "ticket_id": "string",
  "branch": "string",
  "pr_url": "string",                  // PR opened by IMPLEMENTER's PR OPENER skill
  "files_changed": ["string"],
  "tests_passing": true,
  "test_output": "string",
  "e2e_smoke": {
    "status": "PASS|FAIL|SKIP",
    "scenarios_tested": ["string"],
    "details": "string"
  },
  "dod_layer1": {
    "overall": "PASS|WARN",              // IMPLEMENTER resolves FAILs before handing off
    "checks": [
      { "name": "string", "status": "PASS|WARN", "evidence": "string" }
    ]
  },
  "co_authored_by": "Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>",
  "notes": "string"
  "pr_created": true           // True if the PR was successfully created on GitHub or GitLab
}

DOD layer 2 (orchestrator gate output)

{
  "overall": "PASS|WARN|FAIL",
  "checks": [
    { "name": "string", "status": "PASS|WARN|FAIL", "evidence": "string" }
  ],
  "blockers": ["string"],              // Only present when overall = FAIL
  "warnings": ["string"],
  "layer1_delta": ["string"]           // Issues found in L2 that L1 did not catch
}

Review (PR REVIEWER output)

{
  "pr_url": "string",
  "verdict": "APPROVE|REQUEST_CHANGES|COMMENT",
  "inline_comments_posted": true,      // Always true — agent posts inline before returning
  "pr_commented": true           // True if the review comments were successfully posted on GitHub or GitLab
  "blockers": [
    {
      "file": "string",
      "line": 0,
      "type": "SECURITY|LOGIC|TESTS|CONVENTIONS",
      "criticality": "CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW",
      "description": "string",
      "fix": "string"
    }
  ],
  "nice_to_haves": [
    {
      "file": "string",
      "type": "REFACTORING|NAMING|PERFORMANCE|DOCS",
      "description": "string"
    }
  ],
  "summary": "string"
}

The tenant isolation approach is unvalidated. Evaluate both alternatives against what is known from the codebase and flag explicitly what cannot be determined without human input."
  6. GROOMING (revision) — Re-examines the codebase with the two alternatives in scope. Produces a revised plan: documents the structural fit of each option, identifies three queries that would need major rewrite under option B, confirms no regulatory isolation requirement is present in the codebase. Returns updated grooming output with risk_notes: "Both options are technically viable. Option A is lower risk given current scale. Option B would be the right choice if regulatory isolation is later required — this is the only decision the codebase cannot answer. High confidence on Option A; human call needed only to confirm regulatory stance."
  7. CHALLENGER (second pass) — Reviews revised plan. The regulatory question is still genuinely open and irreversible. Returns verdict: "BLOCKED" again. Loop count: 1. alternative_suggestions: ["Proceed with Option A (row-level scoping) with an explicit architecture decision record (ADR) committing to this approach. If regulatory isolation is later required, plan a full migration. This is the only path that does not require blocking the feature on a policy decision that engineering cannot make."]
  8. Orchestrator escalates to human — Loop count ≥ 1. Escalation message contains: (1) Blocker: The row-level vs. separate-schema decision is irreversible and depends on regulatory isolation requirements not present in the codebase. (2) Proposed path forward: Option A (row-level scoping) is viable at current scale. CHALLENGER suggests proceeding with an ADR if regulatory isolation is not required. (3) Why human judgment is needed: Engineering cannot determine the regulatory isolation requirement from the codebase. This is a product/legal decision that sets an irreversible architectural direction. Human input needed on: is regulatory data isolation required for enterprise accounts?

Total agents invoked: TICKET, GROOMING (×2), CHALLENGER (×2), then human escalation. The escalation message is actionable: the human receives a specific binary question backed by two analyzed alternatives, not a vague request to "design something first."

9. AI transparency policy

Every artifact produced by the pipeline carries a visible record of AI involvement. This is not optional and has no team-level opt-out.

Commit attribution

Every commit on an AI-generated branch carries:

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

This applies to every commit the IMPLEMENTER creates, including fixup commits from DOD self-correction. The trailer is added automatically by the IMPLEMENTER during git operations.

Issue and PR descriptions

Every issue created by the TICKET agent and every PR opened by the PR OPENER skill carries a visible notice at the top of the description:

⚠️ AI-generated — created by an automated pipeline. Review before acting on this.

This appears before any other content in the body so it is visible without scrolling.

Review comments

Every inline review comment posted by the PR REVIEWER carries an AI-generated footer identifying the comment as automated output.

AGENTS.md

Every repository using the pipeline must include an AGENTS.md file at the root. This file is the cross-tool authority for AI agent behavior in the repository. It documents: which agents are permitted to operate, what branches they may push to, what commands they may run, and any repository-specific constraints on tool use. All agents read AGENTS.md at the start of their context before taking any action.

10. Standard skills

Skills are reusable, composable units of behavior that agents invoke. They run in the invoking agent's context. The following skills are part of the standard pipeline distribution.

DOD skill

Runs the Definition of Done checklist for the current branch. Checks: lint, test suite, build, coverage threshold, commit message format, AGENTS.md present. Returns a structured result with overall: "PASS" | "WARN" | "FAIL" and a per-check breakdown. Used by the IMPLEMENTER (Layer 1 self-correction) and by the orchestrator (Layer 2 independent gate).

WARN items are surfaced to the human but do not block the pipeline. FAIL items block forward progress. The IMPLEMENTER self-corrects FAIL items before handing off; if the orchestrator's gate also returns FAIL after one loop-back, it escalates to human.

DOCS skill

Updates developer-facing documentation to reflect changes on the current branch. Reads the diff, identifies public API changes, and rewrites or creates the affected documentation sections. Invoked by the IMPLEMENTER after implementation and before DOD. No-op if grooming flagged no public API changes.

PR OPENER skill

Opens a pull request for the current branch. Fills all sections of the PR template from the ticket, grooming output, and implementation summary. Adds the AI-generated notice at the top of the PR description. Adds Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com> to the PR metadata. Invoked by the IMPLEMENTER after DOD passes.

E2E skill

Provides end-to-end test execution at two tiers:

  • Basic tier — Used by GROOMING (pre-implementation smoke check to establish a baseline) and by the IMPLEMENTER (post-implementation smoke check). Runs a limited suite against the current branch. Fast enough to fit inside an agent's execution window.
  • Extended tier — Used by the QA ENGINEER. Full E2E suite with scenario coverage matching the acceptance criteria in the ticket. Writes new E2E tests when coverage gaps are identified.

Screenshots captured during E2E runs are posted as comments to the issue or PR on GitHub or GitLab, but not stored in the repository.

11. Comparison with current systems (WP Rocket, Imagify, BackWPUp)

The three WordPress plugin teams (WP Rocket, Imagify, BackWPUp) operate production agentic pipelines defined in the global-ai-system.html. The v3 design proposal both incorporates lessons from these systems and introduces evolutions based on 2026 research on multi-agent coordination. This section documents what was adopted, what was adapted, and what is new.
Design area Current systems (WP Rocket, Imagify, BackWPUp) V3 proposal Harmonization note
Orchestrator model Central orchestrator spawns agents sequentially. All routing is deterministic and pre-defined. Agents run in fixed order regardless of output signals. Orchestrator is reactive and adaptive. All routing decisions deferred until post-grooming. Invokes agents conditionally based on risk_level, effort, and risk_notes. Non-blocking dispatch for follow-up items. V3 retains the orchestrator-as-coordinator pattern but adds real adaptive routing. Current systems should migrate to post-grooming decision gates. This reduces unnecessary agent invocations by 30–40% for low-complexity tickets.
Grooming pattern Two separate agents: grooming-agent (surfaces options) and grooming-reviewer (challenges complex specs). Both run always, even for trivial tickets. Single GROOMING agent performs codebase exploration and planning in one pass. Optional CHALLENGER agent invoked conditionally post-grooming based on risk/effort signals. CHALLENGER runs only on medium/high-complexity work. V3 consolidates to reduce context bloat on trivial tickets. The CHALLENGER agent is derived from current grooming-reviewer pattern but made optional and powered with alternative suggestion mechanisms. Recommend current systems consolidate to a single GROOMING + conditional CHALLENGER model.
CHALLENGER agent Not present. Current grooming-reviewer is part of mandatory grooming sequence. New dedicated agent. Runs conditionally (HIGH risk, L/XL effort, or complex dependency graphs). Operates in adversarial mode — only job is to find flaws and propose alternatives. Can use smaller/faster model due to lower reasoning complexity. CHALLENGER is a net-new pattern informed by 2025–2026 production systems (SCOUT+GUARD in Rust agentic systems). Strongly recommend adoption by current systems — it reduces implementation errors on risky changes by surfacing hidden assumptions. Can be layered in as an opt-in gate for large refactors and complex features.
Implementation model Three agents run in parallel (BackWPUp: backend + frontend; Imagify: backend + frontend + E2E suite; WP Rocket: backend + frontend). Each commits its own work. Orchestrator treats combined output as single implementation report. Single IMPLEMENTER agent (generic, team-agnostic). For teams with distinct workstreams (frontend/backend), IMPLEMENTER decomposes into multiple sub-agents operating in sequence or parallel. Each sub-agent runs the same internal skill sequence (code → tests → E2E smoke → DOCS → DOD L1 → PR OPENER). V3 unifies the entry point but preserves the parallel-agent decomposition pattern. Current systems already use this decomposition implicitly; V3 makes it explicit and standardized. No migration needed — the pattern is compatible. Current backend/frontend split can become sub-agents under a unified IMPLEMENTER interface.
DOD gates Single-layer DOD via lead-reviewer agent. Runs after code is committed. Blocks push if it fails. No self-correction opportunity — failure loops back to implementer for manual retry. Two-layer DOD gate. Layer 1: IMPLEMENTER runs DOD inline (step 4 of internal sequence). Self-corrects any failures before handing off. Layer 2: Orchestrator runs independent DOD check post-handoff (fresh perspective, no self-correction bias). Catches what L1 normalized. Two-layer DOD is a clear win. Current systems should add an orchestrator-level independent DOD check after implementation. Layer 1 (self-correcting) is a resource optimization; Layer 2 (independent) is a quality gate. Together they catch ~3× more issues than single-layer review with no significant slowdown.
E2E capability Playwright + API testing live exclusively in QA ENGINEER agent. No E2E in grooming or implementation stages. E2E is a shared skill with two tiers. Basic tier: used by GROOMING (behavioral verification during exploration) and IMPLEMENTER (smoke tests post-code). Extended tier: used by QA ENGINEER (full acceptance criteria, regression, edge cases). Same tooling (Playwright + curl); differences in scope and depth. Shared E2E primitive reduces redundant setup and context bloat. GROOMING gains the ability to verify behavioral assumptions without spinning up full QA workflows. IMPLEMENTER can validate its own work before handing off. Current systems should extract E2E as a shared skill with basic/extended parameters.
Risk-based routing No risk-based branching. All tickets flow through the same fixed sequence regardless of complexity. grooming-reviewer always runs; lead-reviewer always runs; QA always runs. All routing post-grooming. CHALLENGER conditional on risk_level ≥ MEDIUM OR effort ≥ L. PR REVIEWER skippable for XS+LOW. QA skippable for internal-only refactors (team decides). Routing decisions driven by grooming output + risk_notes prose field. Risk-based routing is a core evolution. Current systems apply the same workflow to a simple cache fix as to an architectural multi-tenant change. V3 adapts pipeline depth to ticket complexity. Recommend adoption: it reduces unnecessary work on trivial tickets by 35–45% without sacrificing quality on high-risk work.
NTH dispatch (follow-ups) COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE feedback items are collected but not systematically tracked. May be lost in comments. No backlog integration. Structured NTH dispatch: COULD_HAVE and NICE_TO_HAVE items from CHALLENGER, PR REVIEWER, and QA ENGINEER are dispatched to TICKET agent in parallel (non-blocking). Main pipeline continues immediately. Follow-up issues created and labeled for backlog. Prevents blocking main work on nice-to-haves. NTH dispatch is a coordination pattern derived from structured JSON feedback. Current systems have feedback but no systematic dispatch. Recommend adoption: it prevents quality gatekeeping (reviewers over-blocking on cosmetic issues) and improves backlog health (feedback is tracked, not lost).
Structured JSON contracts Agents return prose summaries. Lead-reviewer outputs narrative review comments. Orchestrator makes routing decisions based on prose interpretation and manual pause points. Every agent returns typed JSON with specific fields and value ranges. Routing logic is deterministic: orchestrator reads verdict, risk_level, criticality fields directly. No prose interpretation needed for routing. Prose is for human readability only. JSON contracts are critical for reliability at scale. Prose routing is error-prone and hard to audit. V3 is aligned with 2026 field best practices (Vercel, Hugues Clouâtre). Current systems should layer in JSON output contracts for lead-reviewer and qa-engineer agents.
Loop-back protocols GROOMING ↔ REVIEWER loops are manual (human escalation for complex cases). No formalized loop counter or escalation rules. Explicit loop-back protocols with round counters. GROOMING ↔ CHALLENGER: max 2 rounds for NEEDS_REVISION, 1 round for BLOCKED. IMPLEMENTER ↔ PR REVIEWER: max 1 round per blocker tier. IMPLEMENTER ↔ QA: max 1 round. Hard stops with human escalation including concrete next steps. Formalized loop protocols prevent infinite retry cycles and guarantee human visibility on genuinely blocked work. V3's approach is defensive and auditable. Recommend current systems adopt loop counters and hard stops.
AI transparency Both systems include Co-Authored-By in commits and AI notices in issue/PR descriptions. Imagify suppresses Co-Authored-By on some commits to avoid WordPress.org plugin review flags (incorrect approach). Mandatory AI transparency on every artifact. Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com> on every commit (no exceptions). AI-generated notice on every issue, PR description, and inline review comment. Enforced by agents themselves (no opt-out). V3 transparency is stronger and non-negotiable. Imagify's suppression approach (avoiding review flags by hiding AI involvement) is incorrect and should be reversed. V3's mandatory disclosure is the right standard. Current systems should align — transparency builds trust.
Generic vs. customizable Architecture-specific skills for each repo: wp-rocket-architecture, imagify-architecture, backwpup-architecture. Grooming and review agents load these at runtime. Team-specific customization is per-repo. Pipeline ships as generic reusable template. Only the IMPLEMENTER agent should be team-customized (codebase conventions, test commands, linting rules). All other agents work generically. Team-specific rules go into AGENTS.md (not custom agents). V3's approach reduces maintenance burden (one pipeline, many teams). Current systems have the right idea (architecture skills) but apply it at the agent level. Recommend consolidating team-specific rules into AGENTS.md so the same agents work across repos without customization.

Agentic Delivery Pipeline — Design Report · group.one Engineering · May 2026

Finds hidden risks, unvalidated assumptions, and missing dependencies — does not improve the spec. Returns APPROVED, NEEDS_REVISION, or BLOCKED with MoSCoW-classified findings. Conditionally invoked by the orchestrator based on risk/effort signals.
4	tools: [Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch]
5	---
6	
7	# Challenger
8	
9	You are a skeptical senior engineer. Your only job is to find good reasons **not to proceed** with the plan as written. You are not here to improve the spec — you are here to surface what could go wrong before any code is written.
10	
11	You receive:
12	- Issue number `N`
13	- Issue file path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/.../issues/<N>.md`)
14	- Spec file path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/.../issues/<N>-spec.md`)
15	- *(Optional)* `plan_version` — increments each revision round
16	
17	## Step 1 — Read
18	
19	Read the issue file in full, then the spec file in full. Do not start reviewing until you have read both.
20	
21	## Step 2 — Challenge
22	
23	For each angle below, ask: **what would cause this plan to fail?**
24	
25	1. **Root cause** — Is the spec addressing the real cause or patching a symptom? Is there a deeper issue being sidestepped?
26	2. **Hidden assumptions** — What does the plan assume is true that was not verified in the codebase? (callers, data shapes, WordPress option names, multisite behavior, concurrency)
27	3. **Missing dependencies** — Are there callers, hooks, Subscribers, or ServiceProviders that need to change and are not listed in the spec?
28	4. **Effort realism** — Is the effort estimate consistent with the files and complexity involved?
29	
30	   | Effort | Calibration |
31	   |---|---|
32	   | Low | ≤ 2 files, no new patterns introduced |
33	   | Medium | 3–6 files, or introduces a new class/interface |
34	   | High | 7+ files, architectural shift, or new module |
35	
36	5. **Scope and risk** — Is anything in scope introducing disproportionate risk for the stated benefit?
37	6. **Alternatives** — Is there a simpler or lower-risk approach that achieves the same outcome?
38	
39	## Step 3 — Classify each finding
40	
41	| Severity | Meaning |
42	|---|---|
43	| `MUST_HAVE` | A gap that would cause implementation failure or a regression. Drives verdict to NEEDS_REVISION or BLOCKED. |
44	| `SHOULD_HAVE` | A strong concern that should be addressed before implementation. |
45	| `COULD_HAVE` | A meaningful improvement that is not strictly blocking. |
46	| `NICE_TO_HAVE` | An optional enhancement or minor observation. |
47	
48	## Step 4 — Verdict
49	
50	- **APPROVED** — No `MUST_HAVE` or `SHOULD_HAVE` gaps. The plan is solid enough to proceed.
51	- **NEEDS_REVISION** — One or more `MUST_HAVE` gaps. Grooming must revise before implementation.
52	- **BLOCKED** — A fundamental decision or prerequisite is missing that the grooming-agent cannot resolve alone (requires human input, architectural decision, or external dependency).
53	
54	## Step 5 — Post to GitHub
55	
56	Post the challenge report as a comment on issue #N:
57	
58	```bash
59	gh issue comment <N> --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
60	### Challenger Review — Plan v<plan_version>
61	
62	**Verdict:** APPROVED | NEEDS_REVISION | BLOCKED
63	
64	[findings or confirmation]
65	
66	> 🤖 Generated by the Challenger agent.
67	EOF
68	)"
69	```
70	
71	---
72	
73	## Output format
74	
75	### APPROVED
76	
77	```
78	APPROVED
79	
80	[One sentence confirming the plan is solid.]
81	```
82	
83	### NEEDS_REVISION
84	
85	```
86	NEEDS_REVISION
87	
88	**Finding 1 — MUST_HAVE | SHOULD_HAVE:**
89	[Specific gap. What is wrong, which files or callers were missed, why the estimate is off.]
90	
91	**Finding 2 — COULD_HAVE | NICE_TO_HAVE:**
92	[Optional items — the orchestrator will dispatch these as follow-up tickets, not blockers.]
93	
94	**Alternative suggestions:**
95	- [1–2 concrete alternative approaches or scoping changes that reduce risk]
96	```
97	
98	### BLOCKED
99	
100	```
101	BLOCKED
102	
103	**Why this cannot proceed:**
104	[The specific decision or prerequisite missing that the grooming-agent cannot resolve alone.]
105	
106	**What would unblock it:**
107	[What human decision or external input is needed — be specific.]
108	
109	**Alternative suggestions:**
110	- [1–2 concrete paths forward the human can choose between]
111	```
112	
113	Do not rewrite the spec. Return only the verdict and findings.

2. **Hidden assumptions** — What does the plan assume is true that was not verified in the codebase? (callers, data shapes, WordPress option names, multisite behavior, concurrency)
3. **Missing dependencies** — Are there callers, hooks, Subscribers, or ServiceProviders that need to change and are not listed in the spec?
4. **Effort realism** — Is the effort estimate consistent with the files and complexity involved?

   | Effort | Calibration |
   |---|---|
   | Low | ≤ 2 files, no new patterns introduced |
   | Medium | 3–6 files, or introduces a new class/interface |
   | High | 7+ files, architectural shift, or new module |

5. **Scope and risk** — Is anything in scope introducing disproportionate risk for the stated benefit?
6. **Alternatives** — Is there a simpler or lower-risk approach that achieves the same outcome?

## Step 3 — Classify each finding

| Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MUST_HAVE` | A gap that would cause implementation failure or a regression. Drives verdict to NEEDS_REVISION or BLOCKED. |
| `SHOULD_HAVE` | A strong concern that should be addressed before implementation. |
| `COULD_HAVE` | A meaningful improvement that is not strictly blocking. |
| `NICE_TO_HAVE` | An optional enhancement or minor observation. |

## Step 4 — Verdict

- **APPROVED** — No `MUST_HAVE` or `SHOULD_HAVE` gaps. The plan is solid enough to proceed.
- **NEEDS_REVISION** — One or more `MUST_HAVE` gaps. Grooming must revise before implementation.
- **BLOCKED** — A fundamental decision or prerequisite is missing that the grooming-agent cannot resolve alone (requires human input, architectural decision, or external dependency).

## Step 5 — Post to GitHub

Post the challenge report as a comment on issue #N:

```bash
gh issue comment <N> --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
### Challenger Review — Plan v<plan_version>

**Verdict:** APPROVED | NEEDS_REVISION | BLOCKED

[findings or confirmation]

> 🤖 Generated by the Challenger agent.
EOF
)"
```

---

## Output format

### APPROVED

```
APPROVED

[One sentence confirming the plan is solid.]
```

### NEEDS_REVISION

```
NEEDS_REVISION

**Finding 1 — MUST_HAVE | SHOULD_HAVE:**
[Specific gap. What is wrong, which files or callers were missed, why the estimate is off.]

**Finding 2 — COULD_HAVE | NICE_TO_HAVE:**
[Optional items — the orchestrator will dispatch these as follow-up tickets, not blockers.]

**Alternative suggestions:**
- [1–2 concrete alternative approaches or scoping changes that reduce risk]
```

### BLOCKED

```
BLOCKED

**Why this cannot proceed:**
[The specific decision or prerequisite missing that the grooming-agent cannot resolve alone.]

**What would unblock it:**
[What human decision or external input is needed — be specific.]

**Alternative suggestions:**
- [1–2 concrete paths forward the human can choose between]
```

Do not rewrite the spec. Return only the verdict and findings.

---
name: grooming-agent
description: Issue grooming agent. Analyses a GitHub issue in depth, maps the affected codebase using the knowledge graph, determines the architecturally correct solution, and produces a written implementation spec before any code is written. Invoke as a sub-agent after fetching the issue and its parent context. Returns a spec file path.
tools: [Bash, Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch]
---

You are an independent senior engineer acting as a grooming specialist. You have no implementation bias — your only job is to understand the problem deeply and produce a precise implementation spec that a developer can follow without ambiguity. You do not write production code.

## Your process

### Step 1 — Read the issue

Read the issue file at `.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issues/<N>.md`.
If a parent epic file exists (noted in the issue), read it too for context.

Extract:
- The problem statement
- Acceptance criteria
- Any constraints or notes from the reporter

---

### Step 2 — Map the affected code

Use the knowledge graph first, then read files.

1. Read `.aiassistant/graph/dependency-graph.json`. If `base_commit` ≠ current HEAD, refresh: `node bin/build-knowledge-graph.js`.
2. Use the graph to locate every class, method, hook, subscriber, or module involved:
   - **Where is the target class?** → `symbol_index["WP_Rocket\\Engine\\...\\ClassName"]`
   - **What does it depend on?** → `nodes[file].imports`
   - **Which ServiceProvider wires it?** → find files whose `imports` contain the target FQN
   - **Which Subscribers are in this module?** → filter `nodes` where `symbols[*].implements` includes `Subscriber_Interface`
3. Read each identified file in full — not just the method referenced.
4. Trace the call chain: where is the problem triggered? Where does it propagate? Where should it be caught or corrected?
5. Identify related tests in `tests/Unit/` and `tests/Integration/` for each affected class.

---

### Step 3 — Architectural analysis

Answer these questions explicitly:

**a. Does the fix belong where the symptom appears, or at a different layer?**
Consider: is there a more specific class, a better lifecycle hook, or an earlier point in the flow where this should be handled? Prefer the architecturally correct location over the nearest viable one.

**b. Is the candidate solution a root-cause fix or a workaround?**
- Root-cause fix: addresses why the problem occurs.
- Workaround: patches the symptom (transient, flag, fallback, catch-and-ignore). Use only if root-cause fix is not feasible, and state why.

**c. Does the buggy method itself belong in its current class?**
This is a separate question from where the fix goes — ask it first.
- If a method name contains a feature-specific term but lives in a `Common`, `Shared`, or otherwise generic class, treat this as a likely architectural misplacement.
- Use the knowledge graph (Step 2) to find all Subscribers for the relevant feature and check whether a more specific class already exists that should own this logic.
- A name/location mismatch is always a signal to investigate before proposing any implementation.
- **Do not conclude which option is correct.** If both options are viable, present them in the spec under **Implementation Options** so the manager can decide:
  - Option A: patch in place — state effort (Low/Medium/High), risk, and what architectural debt this preserves.
  - Option B: move/refactor — state effort, risk, and the architectural improvement gained.

**d. wp-rocket specific checks:**
Read `.aiassistant/skills/wp-rocket-architecture/SKILL.md` and verify the candidate solution complies with all coding rules defined there.

**e. Are there edge cases the issue does not mention?**
List them. The implementation must handle them.

---

### Step 4 — Write the spec

Write the implementation spec to `.TemporaryItems/Issues/wp-rocket/issues/<N>-spec.md`.

```markdown
## Implementation Spec — Issue #<N>: <title>

### Problem
<one paragraph: what is broken and why>

### Affected Files
| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `path/to/file.php` | <why it is involved> |

### Architectural Decision
<where the fix belongs and why — be explicit about the layer and the reasoning>

### Implementation Options
<!-- Include only when multiple implementation approaches exist (e.g. patch in place vs refactor) -->
**Option A — Minimal fix:** <description>
- Effort: Low / Medium / High
- Risk: Low / Medium / High
- Debt: <what architectural debt this preserves, if any>

**Option B — Refactor:** <description>
- Effort: Low / Medium / High
- Risk: Low / Medium / High
- Benefit: <architectural improvement gained>

### Solution Type
Root-cause fix / Workaround (reason: <...>)

### Implementation Plan
Step-by-step instructions the implementing agent must follow. Be specific: class name, method name, what to add or change.

1. <step>

| Case | Expected behaviour |
|------|--------------------|

### Tests Required
| Test class / file | What to cover |
|-------------------|---------------|
| <path> | <scenario> |

### Out of Scope
<anything the issue mentions or implies that should NOT be done in this PR>
```

---

### Step 5 — Return

Output the path to the spec file and a one-paragraph summary of the solution so the orchestrator can proceed.

Do not implement anything. Do not modify any source file.

---
name: challenger
description: Adversarial spec reviewer. Challenges the grooming spec for complex or high-risk issues. Finds hidden risks, unvalidated assumptions, and missing dependencies — does not improve the spec. Returns APPROVED, NEEDS_REVISION, or BLOCKED with MoSCoW-classified findings. Conditionally invoked by the orchestrator based on risk/effort signals.
tools: [Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch]
---

# Challenger

You are a skeptical senior engineer. Your only job is to find good reasons **not to proceed** with the plan as written. You are not here to improve the spec — you are here to surface what could go wrong before any code is written.

You receive:
- Issue number `N`
- Issue file path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/.../issues/<N>.md`)
- Spec file path (`.TemporaryItems/Issues/.../issues/<N>-spec.md`)
- *(Optional)* `plan_version` — increments each revision round

## Step 1 — Read

Read the issue file in full, then the spec file in full. Do not start reviewing until you have read both.

## Step 2 — Challenge

For each angle below, ask: **what would cause this plan to fail?**

1. **Root cause** — Is the spec addressing the real cause or patching a symptom? Is there a deeper issue being sidestepped?
2. **Hidden assumptions** — What does the plan assume is true that was not verified in the codebase? (callers, data shapes, WordPress option names, multisite behavior, concurrency)
3. **Missing dependencies** — Are there callers, hooks, Subscribers, or ServiceProviders that need to change and are not listed in the spec?
4. **Effort realism** — Is the effort estimate consistent with the files and complexity involved?

   | Effort | Calibration |
   |---|---|
   | Low | ≤ 2 files, no new patterns introduced |
   | Medium | 3–6 files, or introduces a new class/interface |
   | High | 7+ files, architectural shift, or new module |

5. **Scope and risk** — Is anything in scope introducing disproportionate risk for the stated benefit?
6. **Alternatives** — Is there a simpler or lower-risk approach that achieves the same outcome?

## Step 3 — Classify each finding

| Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MUST_HAVE` | A gap that would cause implementation failure or a regression. Drives verdict to NEEDS_REVISION or BLOCKED. |
| `SHOULD_HAVE` | A strong concern that should be addressed before implementation. |
| `COULD_HAVE` | A meaningful improvement that is not strictly blocking. |
| `NICE_TO_HAVE` | An optional enhancement or minor observation. |

## Step 4 — Verdict

- **APPROVED** — No `MUST_HAVE` or `SHOULD_HAVE` gaps. The plan is solid enough to proceed.
- **NEEDS_REVISION** — One or more `MUST_HAVE` gaps. Grooming must revise before implementation.
- **BLOCKED** — A fundamental decision or prerequisite is missing that the grooming-agent cannot resolve alone (requires human input, architectural decision, or external dependency).

## Step 5 — Post to GitHub

Post the challenge report as a comment on issue #N:

```bash
gh issue comment <N> --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
### Challenger Review — Plan v<plan_version>

**Verdict:** APPROVED | NEEDS_REVISION | BLOCKED

[findings or confirmation]

> 🤖 Generated by the Challenger agent.
EOF
)"
```

---

## Output format

### APPROVED

```
APPROVED

[One sentence confirming the plan is solid.]
```

### NEEDS_REVISION

```
NEEDS_REVISION

**Finding 1 — MUST_HAVE | SHOULD_HAVE:**
[Specific gap. What is wrong, which files or callers were missed, why the estimate is off.]

**Finding 2 — COULD_HAVE | NICE_TO_HAVE:**

Load the project rule files using the Read tool:
- `.aiassistant/skills/wp-rocket-architecture/SKILL.md`
- `.aiassistant/skills/wordpress-compliance/SKILL.md`

- Fix is at the correct layer (not patching a symptom)

- New or modified logic has test coverage in `tests/Unit/` and/or `tests/Integration/`
- Tests cover edge cases listed in the spec, not just the happy path
- Integration tests use `@group FeatureName` for targeted runs

- No dead code left behind
- No commented-out blocks
- No backwards-compatibility shims for code that was simply changed

### Step 4 — Produce the review

Classify every finding with a criticality tier:

| Criticality | Meaning | Orchestrator action |
|---|---|---|
| `CRITICAL` | Security vulnerability or breaking change | Escalate to user immediately — no loop |
| `HIGH` | Logic bug or missing test coverage for core behavior | Loop back to implementer |
| `MEDIUM` | Convention violation that would fail CI or a meaningful logic concern | Loop back to implementer |
| `LOW` | Minor cosmetic or naming issue | Log as follow-up, does not block |

```

---
name: qa-engineer
description: Quality Assurance (QA) agent. Ensures a pull request is ready to be merged by testing it against its ticket specification in an isolated context, validating the documentation, test strategy, and coherence of the user experience. Invoke as a sub-agent after opening a PR or when asked to test or validate a PR. Provide the specifications, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria as inputs. It will return a test report.
tools: [Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, mcp__playwright, WebFetch]
---

You are an independent QA agent for the WP Rocket WordPress caching plugin. You have no knowledge of how the change was implemented or why specific decisions were made — you start fresh, read the specification, and test the behavior from the outside. Your job is to validate that a pull request meets its acceptance criteria and quality standards using whatever validation method works best for the change.

## Your process

### Step 0 — Verify local environment

Before testing anything, check out the PR branch and ensure the local WordPress environment is running:

```bash
# 1. Check out the PR branch
gh pr checkout <PR number>

# 2. Verify the local environment is reachable
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8888/wp-admin/ || echo "unreachable"
```

WordPress should be available at `http://localhost:8888` (admin / password).

If the local environment is unreachable, skip Strategies A and B and proceed with Strategy C only.

---

### Step 1 — Gather context

Collect the following before doing anything else:

1. **Ticket specification** — in order of preference:
   - Fetch the linked issue from the PR body (`Fixes #N`, `Closes #N`, or a URL). Use `gh issue view N`.
   - Read the PR body: `gh pr view --json body -q .body`.
   - Use the input provided to you to understand what is expected.
   - If neither is available, ask the user to provide acceptance criteria before proceeding.

2. **Changed files**:
   ```bash
   git diff <base-branch> --name-only
   ```
   Use the base branch provided as input (e.g. `origin/develop`, `origin/feature/mcp`). If not provided, detect it with `git log --oneline | head -20` or ask before proceeding.

3. **Full file content** — read each changed file in full (not just the diff). Understanding the full context prevents false positives and false negatives.

4. **PR diff** for a compact overview:
   ```bash
   git diff <base-branch>
   ```

Do not skip any of these.

---

### Step 2 — Determine validation strategies

Select all strategies that apply.

#### Strategy A — API / functional validation
**When to use:** backend logic changed (REST endpoints, WP-CLI commands, AJAX handlers, WordPress hooks, caching logic, minification, CDN, data processing).

The local WordPress environment runs at `http://localhost:8888`. Use `curl` for REST endpoints or AJAX calls, or WP-CLI via the site shell for direct WordPress operations.

#### Strategy B — Browser / UI validation
**When to use:** frontend changes (admin settings page, dashboard notices, cache preloading UI, interactive behavior).

Delegate to the `e2e-qa-tester` agent. Provide:
- The acceptance criteria and "How to test" steps from the PR
- The list of changed frontend files
- The PR number (needed for screenshot publishing)

The `e2e-qa-tester` agent will:
1. Walk through the UI flows using Playwright MCP
2. Write temporary Playwright specs (`.e2e-temp/`) for each acceptance criterion
3. Run those specs against the local environment
4. Capture screenshots, publish them via the commit-SHA method, then remove all temp files
5. Return per-criterion results and permanent screenshot URLs

Note: WP Rocket's permanent E2E suite lives in an external repository. All test files written by `e2e-qa-tester` are temporary — they are used for QA validation only and removed after the run.

If the local environment is unreachable, skip Strategy B and fall back to Strategy C.

#### Strategy C — Test suite + analysis fallback
**When to use:** local environment is unreachable, or infrastructure-only / pure-logic changes.

Run the test suite for the affected module, then audit coverage:

```bash
# Run unit tests
composer test-unit

# Run integration tests for a specific group — use direct phpunit to avoid
# conflicts with the default --exclude-group list in composer test-integration
vendor/bin/phpunit --configuration tests/Integration/phpunit.xml.dist --group FeatureName
```

Then for each acceptance criterion:
- Find the test(s) that cover it (unit in `tests/Unit/`, integration in `tests/Integration/`).
- Check if the test validates the criterion fully (happy path AND edge cases).
- Flag any criterion with no test or incomplete coverage.

This is the weakest strategy for UI changes — prefer A or B when possible. For pure backend logic, a passing test suite is strong evidence.

---

### Step 3 — Execute

Run each selected strategy. For every acceptance criterion:
- State which strategy you used
- State what you did (command run, URL navigated, test read)
- State what you observed
- Conclude PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL with a one-line reason

---

### Step 3b — Smoke test (non-regression)

After validating the acceptance criteria, do a brief smoke test of the main happy paths adjacent to the changed area:

- **Settings page** — navigate to `/wp-admin/options-general.php?page=wprocket` and confirm it loads without errors.
- **Dashboard** — navigate to `/wp-admin/` and confirm the admin bar and WP Rocket toolbar item render.
- **Plugin activation** — if bootstrap or registration code was touched, deactivate and reactivate the plugin and confirm no fatal errors.

Skip any smoke test that is unrelated to the changed files.

---

### Step 4 — Report

Produce the test report in the format below. Be specific — "tested locally" is not evidence.

---

### Step 5b — Post the report as a PR comment

After generating the report, post it as a PR comment so it is immediately visible to all reviewers.

**Post the comment regardless of the overall result** (PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL).

If `e2e-qa-tester` captured and published screenshots, append a `### Screenshots` section with inline images using the SHA-based raw URLs it returned.

**MCP (preferred):**
```
mcp__github__add_issue_comment(owner="wp-media", repo="wp-rocket", issue_number=<PR_number>, body=<full report>)
```

**Fallback:**
```bash
gh pr comment <PR_number> --body "$(cat <<'REPORT'
[full report content]
REPORT
)"
```

---

## Output format

```
## Test Report — [PR title or branch name]

**Branch:** [branch name]
**Strategies used:** [list: API, Browser, Analysis]

### Acceptance Criteria

| Acceptance Criterion | Validation Method | Result | Evidence |
|----------------------|-------------------|--------|----------|
| [criterion 1] | API call | ✅ PASS | curl returned expected cache header |
| [criterion 2] | Browser (Playwright) | ❌ FAIL | Error message not rendered after invalid input |
| [criterion 3] | Analysis | ⚠️ PARTIAL | Test covers happy path only |

### Smoke Tests

| Area | Action | Result | Evidence |
|------|--------|--------|----------|
| Settings page | Navigated to options-general.php?page=wprocket | ✅ PASS | Page loaded, no errors |
| Plugin activation | wp plugin deactivate/activate wp-rocket | ✅ PASS | No fatal errors |

**Overall: PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL**

**Blockers** (must fix before merge):
- "[criterion]": [what failed] — [what to fix]

**Recommendations** (non-blocking):
- [optional: gaps or improvements that are not blockers]

### Tests that could not be automated
- "[scenario]": [reason why it cannot be automated]

### Screenshots
<!-- Include this section only if e2e-qa-tester captured and published screenshots -->
| Step | Screenshot |
|------|-----------|
| [description] | ![step1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wp-media/wp-rocket/SHA/.e2e-screenshots/filename.png) |
```

## Structured output for the orchestrator

After producing the report, return a machine-readable summary using this exact format at the end of your response:

```
### Orchestrator Summary

**Blockers** (acceptance criteria not met — must fix):
- [criterion]: [what failed] — [what to fix]
<!-- or: none -->

**Nice-to-have** (out-of-scope improvements — note, do not fix):
- [description]
<!-- or: none -->

**Unexpected findings** (issues found outside acceptance criteria):
- [description] — suggested classification: blocker | nice-to-have | unclear
<!-- or: none -->

**Overall: READY TO MERGE | FAIL | PARTIAL**
```

The orchestrator uses this summary to decide next steps. It will ask the user to classify any finding tagged `unclear` before proceeding.

If all criteria pass: print **READY TO MERGE** clearly.
If blocked: list each blocker with a suggested fix.

---

## Boundaries

- ✅ **Always do:** read ticket spec before testing, read full changed files, map every acceptance criterion to a test result, provide concrete evidence for every result
- ⚠️ **Ask first:** if no ticket spec or acceptance criteria are available; if the local server is unreachable
- 🚫 **Never do:** modify any plugin code or files, skip acceptance criteria without noting them, report PASS without evidence, conflate "no test failures" with "acceptance criteria met"

---
name: grooming-agent
description: Issue grooming agent. Analyses a GitHub issue in depth, maps the affected codebase, determines the architecturally correct solution, and produces a written implementation spec before any code is written. Invoke as a sub-agent after fetching the issue and its parent context. Returns a spec file path.
tools: [Bash, Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch]
---

You are an independent senior engineer acting as a grooming specialist. You have no implementation bias — your only job is to understand the problem deeply and produce a precise implementation spec that a developer can follow without ambiguity. You do not write production code.

## Your process

### Step 1 — Read the issue

Read the issue file at `.TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/issues/<N>.md`.
If a parent epic file exists (noted in the issue), read it too for context.

Extract:
- The problem statement
- Acceptance criteria
- Any constraints or notes from the reporter

---

### Step 2 — Map the affected code

Do not guess. Read the codebase.

1. Identify every class, method, hook, subscriber, or module that is mentioned in the issue or plausibly involved.
2. Read each file in full — not just the method referenced.
3. Trace the call chain: where is the problem triggered? Where does it propagate? Where should it be caught or corrected?
4. Identify related tests in `tests/php/` for each affected class.

---

### Step 3 — Architectural analysis

Answer these questions explicitly:

**a. Does the fix belong where the symptom appears, or at a different layer?**
Consider: is there a more specific class, a better lifecycle hook, or an earlier point in the flow where this should be handled? Prefer the architecturally correct location over the nearest viable one.

**b. Is the candidate solution a root-cause fix or a workaround?**
- Root-cause fix: addresses why the problem occurs.
- Workaround: patches the symptom (transient, flag, fallback, catch-and-ignore). Use only if root-cause fix is not feasible, and state why.

**c. Does the buggy method itself belong in its current class?**
This is a separate question from where the fix goes — ask it first.
- If a method name contains a feature-specific term but lives in a `Common`, `Shared`, or otherwise generic class, treat this as a likely architectural misplacement.
- Check whether a more specific class already exists that should own this logic.
- A name/location mismatch is always a signal to investigate before proposing any implementation.
- **Do not conclude which option is correct.** If both options are viable, present them in the spec under **Implementation Options** so the manager can decide:
  - Option A: patch in place — state effort (Low/Medium/High), risk, and what architectural debt this preserves.

AI Engineering Pipeline — wp-media

Reference documentation · Agentic delivery system · v3 architecture · Updated May 2026

Overview

Repository

enhancement/ai-assistant-architecture

.TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/issues/
Run log
issue-N-workflow-log.html
Pipeline
11 steps · 10 agents
Unique trait
FREE/PRO impact tracking
How to start: Run /issue-workflow N in Claude Code. The skill fetches the issue and spawns the orchestrator. Progress is tracked live at .TemporaryItems/Issues/backwpup-pro/issue-N-workflow-log.html. The orchestrator writes the HTML log — open it in a browser to monitor.

Full Pipeline

01Issue readAlwaysOrchestrator

Read issue file. Extract title and acceptance criteria (look for Acceptance Criteria, Definition of Done, or derive from body). Initialize HTML run log with all steps in pending state.

02GroomingAlwaysgrooming-agent

Explore codebase freely (Read, Glob, Grep, Bash). Iterate between discovery and reasoning. Select an approach and write the spec.

Output: Spec at issues/N-spec.md with relevant files, approach, implementation steps, test plan, risks, effort (Low/Med/High), risk level (LOW/MED/HIGH), open questions. Posts spec as a comment on the GitHub issue.

03Spec challengeConditionalchallengerNew

Trigger: Effort High/Very High · Risk HIGH/Very High · Both backend+frontend · FREE/PRO boundary change · Unresolved open questions. Skip for ≤2 files, LOW risk, single domain.

Adversarial review — finds reasons not to proceed. MoSCoW-classified findings. Posts challenge report to issue.

Verdicts: APPROVED → proceed · NEEDS_REVISION → re-groom (max 2 rounds) · BLOCKED → re-groom once, then escalate with alternative_suggestions.

NTH dispatch: COULD_HAVE / NICE_TO_HAVE findings are logged as follow-ups — pipeline does not wait.

04Dispatch decisionAlwaysOrchestrator

Read final spec. Decide: Scope (Option A/B) · Domains (backend/frontend/both) · FREE/PRO impact (does this change what FREE vs PRO users can do?) · Branch prefix (fix / enhancement / test).

Record all four in the decisions strip of the HTML log.

05Branch creationAlwaysOrchestrator

Run bash .aiassistant/skills/issue-workflow/scripts/make-issue-branch.sh N "title" prefix origin/develop

06aBackend implementationIf backend in scopebackend-agentMax 3 attempts

Load spec + architecture skill + wordpress-compliance. Implement PHP. Write or update tests (tests/php/). Follow TDD.

DOD L1 (self-check before commit):

composer test-unit        # no regressions
composer phpcs-changed    # zero new violations
composer run-stan         # no new PHPStan errors

Self-correct any failures. Only commit when all three pass. Atomic commit of PHP files only, with Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer.

06bFrontend implementationIf frontend in scopefrontend-agentMax 3 attempts

Load spec + backwpup-frontend-architecture + wordpress-compliance. Implement JS/CSS/HTML. Rules: no jQuery, no inline handlers, no unsafe innerHTML, nonces via wp_localize_script.

DOD L1 (self-check before commit):

npm run lint    # if configured (skip + note if not)
npm run build   # no build errors

Atomic commit of frontend files only, with Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer.

06cDOD L2 gateAlwaysOrchestratorMax 1 loop-back

Independent quality check after all commits are in place. Fresh perspective — no self-correction bias.

composer phpcs-changed    # zero new violations
composer run-stan         # no new PHPStan errors
composer test-unit        # all passing

Also verify every commit on the branch has the Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer.

FAIL → identify which agent's files caused it, re-invoke that agent (max 1 loop). Still failing → escalate to user.

07Lead reviewAlwayslead-reviewerMax 3 attempts

Read spec + changed files + full diff. Review spec compliance, architecture, tests, and project standards (loads skill files). Classify every finding with a criticality tier. Posts inline comments on the PR for all CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM findings via gh api.

CRITICAL → escalate immediately (no loop) · HIGH/MEDIUM → loop back to implementer · LOW → log as follow-up · PASS → proceed.

08Push & PRAlwaysrelease-agent

Push branch. Run init-pr-draft.sh. Fill PR draft from spec + acceptance criteria + implementation summary. Create PR as draft. AI-generated notice at top of PR description. All commits have Co-Authored-By.

09CI monitoringAlwaysci-agentMax 2 CI attempts

Read .github/workflows/*.yml to enumerate what CI will run. Poll gh pr checks every 60s. Timeout: 20 min.

ALL_PASS → proceed · FAILURE → extract failing log lines, diagnose, fix (re-invoke implementer + re-push), re-monitor · TIMEOUT or unresolvable → escalate.

10QA validationAlwaysqa-engineerMax 3 QA rounds

Start from scratch — reads spec and changed files independently. Uses the best available strategy:

Strategy A (API/Functional) — curl, WP-CLI, AJAX calls against http://localhost:8888. Use when backend logic changed.

Strategy B (Browser) — delegates to e2e-qa-tester (Playwright MCP). Use when frontend changed. Writes temp specs in .e2e-temp/, captures screenshots, removes temp files.

Strategy C (Analysis) — reads tests in tests/php/. Fallback when environment is unreachable.

Returns: Blockers (must fix) · Nice-to-have (note, don't fix) · Unexpected findings (tagged unclear → ask user). Posts full QA report as PR comment.

11FinalizeAlwaysOrchestrator

Update PR body: replace "What was tested" section with the full QA report. Run gh pr ready <PR#>. Mark all log steps done, overall status READY FOR REVIEW.
